docs.title: django-offsite-backup
docs.text:
Encrypted, immutable off-site backups of a Django project's databases, media and deployment configuration — written by the machine they protect, readable only off it. The same passes run on a server with no Django project, from the offsite-backup command (Without Django).

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {
    'PREFIX': 'acme/prod',
    'STORE': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
        'ENDPOINT_URL': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT', ''),
        'BUCKET': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_BUCKET', ''),
        'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
        'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
    },
    'ENCRYPTION': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
        'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
    },
    'DATABASES': {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource'},
}

python manage.py backup_offsite                    # a whole pass, now
python manage.py backup_offsite --without-media --reason deploy   # before a migration
python manage.py backup_check                      # the morning check
python manage.py backup_status                     # each kind's age, for a monitor
python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest     # get it back
python manage.py backup_drill                      # prove it comes back, monthly

docs.title: What a pass does
docs.text:
1. Dumps every database — PostgreSQL with pg_dump, MySQL and MariaDB with mysqldump --single-transaction, SQLite with its online backup API — compresses it with zstd, encrypts it with age (or pyrage, the same format without the binary) to a public key, and uploads it. A database that fails does not cost the others their night.
  2. Packs the media — a directory, a Docker volume, an S3 bucket or any Django storage — into volumes of whole files (4 GiB by default), each a complete tar on its own with a manifest beside it, streamed through encryption one at a time — media larger than the free disk works, and one file comes back without the rest.
  3. Archives the deployment directory and the environment rebuilt from a list of names, last: a configuration object for a stamp means every part before it went up.
  4. Only then rotates — counted in whole UTC nights, never in objects or age — in every store, when there are several, each by its own window.
  5. Says what happened in a chat (Telegram, or through your django-aiogram bot) or to a webhook, in one format a phone shows at a glance.

On S3 every object is uploaded with an Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode, and the lock is read back after the upload: an object locked less than asked fails the pass. A stolen write key can neither read a backup (it has no private key) nor delete one (the lock refuses it). Security model spells out exactly what that does and does not cover.

docs.title: Off, on, or refused
docs.text: A machine with no store credentials is off — a recipient alone switches nothing on: every command says "nothing to do" and exits 0, which is what a developer laptop wants. A machine that has the store credentials and lacks something else is partly configured and is refused by name (E001) — a production machine that lost one variable must not stop backing up in silence. A blank value, 0 or [''] counts as unset. Settings has the rule.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Installation

    The extras, the binaries the image needs, and a first pass in five minutes.

  • S3 providers

    Creating a bucket that can actually hold a locked backup — Object Lock is only possible at creation, and a missing default rule breaks every large object.

  • Deploy integration

    One command before the migration; non-zero stops the deploy while the live release keeps serving.

  • Restore

    Step by step, and the monthly drill that restores the newest backup into a throwaway database, counts every table and says so.

  • Without Django

    The same passes on a plain server: a TOML file, offsite-backup run, cron.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Python 3.10–3.14, and Django 5.2+ for the Django layer. The base install pulls nothing; Django and each driver are extras ([django], [cli], [s3], [telegram], [webhook], [aiogram]). The binaries a pass runs — pg_dump, zstd, age — are checked by manage.py check (E003) rather than discovered at 03:00.

Released under the MIT licence.

docs.title: AI assistants
docs.text: Coding agents wire this package into a project the way a person would — by reading the docs — and the mistakes they make are the expensive kind: a private key on the server, a test suite posting to the team's chat, a bucket without Object Lock. This page is the brief to hand them.

docs.title: Paste this in
docs.text:
Short enough for a system prompt or a CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / .cursor/rules file:

Project uses django-offsite-backup 0.4. Rules:

- Install with the extras the configuration names, nothing inferred:
  `django-offsite-backup[s3,telegram]` for an S3 store and Telegram messages,
  `[s3,aiogram]` to send through the project's django-aiogram bot. Add
  'offsite_backup' to INSTALLED_APPS. It has no models and no migrations.
- The image that runs a pass needs the binaries: pg_dump (major >= the
  PostgreSQL server's), zstd, age. Not tar. Install them in the worker's image
  AND the image the deploy pass runs in.
- Settings are one dict, OFFSITE_BACKUP, in settings.py. Read EVERY credential
  from the environment with a default of '' — os.environ.get('X', '') — never
  os.environ['X'] and never a placeholder value. Empty means "backups off on this
  machine", which is what developer laptops and CI want.
- The age RECIPIENTS is a public key and may be read from the environment or
  written into settings; it does not switch backups on by itself. Read it with
  the same idiom, as a plain string:
  'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENTS', '') — a string splits
  on commas (and between age1 keys on whitespace). Do not wrap it in a list or
  split it yourself. Blank values (None, '', 0, [''] ) count as unset, so E001
  still names a missing variable.
- Backend paths, exactly:
  offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store / offsite_backup.stores.filesystem.DirectoryStore
  offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli
  offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource
  offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource / offsite_backup.media.s3.S3Source
  offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource
  offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier
  offsite_backup.notifiers.django_aiogram.TopicNotifier
  offsite_backup.notifiers.log.LogNotifier
  offsite_backup.notifiers.webhook.WebhookNotifier   ([webhook] extra)
- NEVER put an age private key (AGE-SECRET-KEY-...) on the server, in settings,
  in .env, in CI variables, or in the repository. RECIPIENTS takes public keys
  (age1...). The private key is generated on a person's machine with age-keygen
  and kept in their password manager. E008 refuses a private key in RECIPIENTS.
  Do not generate a key pair for the user: tell them to run age-keygen and give
  you the public half.
- The S3 bucket must be created WITH Object Lock (it cannot be enabled later)
  and given a default retention rule COMPLIANCE, days == STORE['LOCK_DAYS']
  (13). Keep RETENTION['KEEP_NIGHTS'] (14) greater than LOCK_DAYS. Never
  suggest GOVERNANCE mode. Never "fix" E005/E006 by setting LOCK_DAYS to 0
  without the user explicitly accepting backups that the server can delete.
- PREFIX is required ('<project>/<env>', e.g. 'acme/prod'). Rotation never
  leaves it.
- Scheduling: Celery -> CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {**beat_schedule(), ...} from
  offsite_backup.schedule.celery, with CELERY_IMPORTS including
  'offsite_backup.schedule.celery' and the beat in UTC. taskiq ->
  register(broker) from offsite_backup.schedule.taskiq. cron -> 03:00 UTC
  `manage.py backup_offsite --reason nightly`, 09:00 UTC `manage.py backup_check`.
  The guard needs GUARD['CACHE'] to be a cache shared by every worker (Redis,
  Memcached, database) — not LocMemCache (W003) — or, in a project without a
  shared cache, GUARD = {'BACKEND': 'database'} (a PostgreSQL advisory lock).
  Celery's beat entries are in CELERY_TIMEZONE; do not switch a project's beat
  to UTC without asking (it moves every other entry) — pass local hours to
  beat_schedule() instead. taskiq retries need SimpleRetryMiddleware on the
  broker.
- Deploy: ALWAYS write the full line
  `python manage.py backup_offsite --without-media --reason deploy` — both
  flags; without --reason the pass reads "By hand" and its failure does not
  say the deploy stops. Run it on the NEW image BEFORE `migrate`, and let a
  non-zero exit stop the deploy. Do not add `|| true`. Mount the deployment
  directory read-only into the service that runs it AND into the worker.
- Validate with `python manage.py check` and `python manage.py check --deploy`.
  Missing mounts (W005, E009 for a REQUIRED path) are reported by
  `check --deploy` only — run it in each service that runs a pass (the deploy's
  and the worker); a plain check is quiet about paths on purpose. Treat offsite_backup.E0xx/W0xx as the spec. Do not silence an error; only
  W001 (directory store) may be silenced, and only where the user chose it.
- Tests must never notify. pytest is covered by the package's plugin
  automatically, pytest-xdist workers included; with Django's runner set
  TEST_RUNNER = 'offsite_backup.testing.OffsiteBackupTestRunner'. If the
  project ALREADY has its own runner, do not replace it: mix the behaviour in,
  mixin first — class Runner(OffsiteBackupRunnerMixin, ExistingRunner). This
  also covers `manage.py test --parallel` workers (spawn/forkserver). If that
  runner sets its own parallel_test_suite, make it a subclass of
  offsite_backup.testing.SilencedParallelTestSuite. Do not give CI test jobs
  the production notifier token or store keys. In
  tests use offsite_backup.testing: use_fake_s3(FakeS3()), Passthrough as the
  ENCRYPTION backend with COMPRESS [], capture() to assert on messages,
  media_tree() for media. Passthrough is for tests only (W002).
- Restore: `manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --into DIR` with the
  private key in AGE_IDENTITY or --identity FILE, run by a person on their own
  machine. Never write code that stores the identity on the server.
- The restore drill (`manage.py backup_drill`) restores into
  DRILL['DATABASE'], which must be a throwaway database — never an alias, host+
  port+name of a live one (refused; E011). It needs the private key: do not
  schedule it on the production worker unless the user explicitly accepts the
  key there; prefer a separate machine running `offsite-backup drill`. Its
  schedule is off by default — beat_schedule(drill=(1, 5, 0)) /
  register(broker, drill='0 5 1 * *') only when asked.
- Monitoring: `manage.py backup_status` exits 1 when a kind is stale, 2 when
  the store is unreadable; `--prometheus FILE` for a textfile collector.
- A server with no Django project uses the `offsite-backup` command with a TOML
  setting (same keys as OFFSITE_BACKUP, secrets as ${VAR} from the environment
  or --env-file, never literal), PostgresSource CONNECTIONS for its databases,
  and cron with flock. Install `django-offsite-backup[cli,s3,...]` with pipx.

docs.title: Prompts that work
docs.text:
Wire it in. "Add django-offsite-backup to this project: S3 store with credentials from BACKUP_S3_* variables, age recipient from BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT, PostgreSQL default, media from MEDIA_ROOT, the deploy/ directory as configuration, Telegram from BACKUP_TELEGRAM_*. Add the Celery beat entries, the pre-migration step to our deploy script, the read-only mount on web and worker, the binaries to the Dockerfile, and OffsiteBackupTestRunner. Do not generate keys. Show me manage.py check output with the variables unset." — the last sentence is the test that the laptop stays "off".

Review a wiring. "Check our OFFSITE_BACKUP settings and deploy script against the django-offsite-backup docs: credentials from the environment with '' defaults, no private key anywhere, backup before migrate with a failing exit stopping the deploy, mounts on both services, notifier silenced in tests."

Prepare a bucket. "Give me the AWS CLI commands to create a bucket with Object Lock and a default COMPLIANCE rule of 13 days on , and a least-privilege policy for the backup key under prefix acme/prod/. Do not run them."

docs.title: What to check after an agent is done
docs.text:
• grep -rn "AGE-SECRET-KEY" . finds nothing — in the repository, the CI configuration or the server's .env.
  • python manage.py check with the backup variables unset reports no offsite_backup code (the machine is off); with them set, none but warnings you chose.
  • python manage.py check --deploy on the server: no E004, E005, E006.
  • The deploy script stops when backup_offsite exits non-zero — try it once with a wrong bucket name on staging — and its line carries --reason deploy.
  • The test job's environment holds no production notifier token, and a project with its own test runner mixes in OffsiteBackupRunnerMixin rather than losing it.
  • Someone has restored a backup — Restore.

docs.title: 0.4.1 — 2026-11-04
docs.text: • The Telegram token and the webhook URL stay out of the HTTP client's log. httpx2 logs every request at INFO with its URL, and the Bot API carries the token in the path: wherever the logging shows INFO for httpx2 (the command line does), the token was written to the journal. A filter on the client's logger now replaces both with <redacted>, whoever configured the logging. Rotate a bot token that ran under 0.4.0's command line, or under a Django project logging httpx2 at INFO.

docs.title: 0.4.0 — 2026-11-04
docs.text: Nothing to edit in a Django project; Upgrading has the behaviours that move and what to consider turning on.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
The restore drill. manage.py backup_drill (and offsite-backup drill, run_drill()) downloads the newest whole backup, decrypts it, restores every database into the throwaway DRILL['DATABASE'] — never a live one: a target reaching a database the pass dumps is refused, and is E011 under check --deploy — counts every table there and live, opens every media volume and the configuration archive, says the outcome through the notifiers and empties the target. A schedule entry for it in both adapters, off unless asked (beat_schedule(drill=...), register(broker, drill=...)). Restore.

A webhook notifier. WebhookNotifier ([webhook]) POSTs the outcome as JSON beside its text, signed with HMAC-SHA256 when given a SECRET, retried on a network error, a 429 or a 5xx; E010 checks its options. Notifications.

The age of every kind, for a monitor. manage.py backup_status (offsite-backup status, freshness()) answers each kind's newest whole backup and its age, exits 1 when one is stale and 2 when the store cannot be read, and writes a Prometheus textfile with --prometheus. Monitoring.

Without Django. The offsite-backup command runs the same passes, checks, restore and drill on a server with no Django project, from a TOML file whose top level is OFFSITE_BACKUP, with ${NAME} read from the environment and --env-file files. PostgresSource takes its connections from CONNECTIONS. Django is the [django] extra; the core imports without it. Without Django.

docs.title: Sources and stores
docs.text:
More sources. MySQL and MariaDB (mysqldump --single-transaction, the password in a private option file) and SQLite (the online backup API) beside PostgreSQL (Databases); a Docker volume the worker does not mount, read through a container that never starts, and any Django storage, streamed a block at a time (Media).

Manifests and selective restore. Every media volume has a sealed manifest beside it — path, size and SHA-256 of each file. backup_restore --path brings back one file or one folder, downloading only the volumes that hold it and checking every file against its hash; --database ALIAS brings back one database (Restore).

Several stores. STORE takes a list: every pass goes to each store, each read back, locked and rotated on its own; a store that refuses fails the pass by its name, never a silent partial (Several stores).

pyrage. encryption.pyrage.Pyrage seals in age's format without the binary; either opens what the other sealed (Encryption).

Every new source runs under the drill and the command line too — MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite are counted and emptied by the drill like PostgreSQL; a Django storage needs a Django project and is refused by name without one (Without Django).

docs.title: 0.3.0 — 2026-11-04
docs.text:
Nothing to edit on upgrade; Upgrading has the two checks that moved.

Path checks only where a pass runs. W005 — a media ROOT, an optional CONFIG path or the RENDER_ENV file not found — was printed by every container that ran manage.py on a deploy (the web service, a migrate), though none of them runs a pass or mounts the deployment directory. It is now a deploy check, beside E009: check --deploy, run where the pass runs, reports it, and a plain check or migrate does not. The pass logs each path it leaves out (Configuration path not found; left out, Media directory not found), so the worker says it too. System checks.

E010 for notifier options. A TOPIC_ID that is not an integer — one check shared by both Telegram notifiers — and a DELIVERY other than direct/queue are E010 instead of E001. System checks.

docs.title: 0.2.0 — 2026-11-03
docs.text:
Nothing breaks: every new setting defaults to 0.1's behaviour. What to consider turning on is on Upgrading.

Fixed: tests notified from parallel workers. Under manage.py test --parallel, workers started with spawn (macOS) or forkserver (Linux, Python 3.14) did not inherit the runner's silence, and a configured notifier could post. The runner now sets OFFSITE_BACKUP_SILENCE=1 for the run, which notify.silenced() honours in every process, and its parallel_test_suite is SilencedParallelTestSuite, whose process_setup silences each worker. OffsiteBackupRunnerMixin brings both to a project's own runner. The pytest plugin covers pytest-xdist workers, each of which loads it. Testing.

Blank values are unset. None, blank strings, 0 and lists made only of those count as unset for required options, so E001 names them — [os.environ.get('X', '')] and int(os.environ.get('X') or 0) no longer pass for configured. Blank items are dropped from PATHS, INCLUDE/EXCLUDE and ALIASES lists. RECIPIENTS takes a string or a list; a string splits on commas, newlines and, between age1… keys, whitespace. Settings.

TopicNotifier: queued delivery and a bot factory. DELIVERY: 'queue' sends through bot.send — the queue a bot container consumes, with no token in the worker; 'direct' (default) is bot.send_raw, as before. BOT_FACTORY names a callable returning any object with send_raw/send. Both Telegram notifiers share ChatNotifier: TOPIC_ID is validated on both, and None, blank or 0 means the main thread. Notifications.

S3 client options. ADDRESSING_STYLE (auto, path, virtual), SIGNATURE_VERSION and VERIFY (a bool, or a CA bundle's path) on S3Store and S3Source. S3 providers.

DEFAULT_REASON. The reason backup_offsite uses without --reason (default manual). --without-media without an explicit --reason prints a one-line notice suggesting --reason deploy. Deploy integration.

STRICT and REQUIRED. REQUIRED on CONFIG (True, or a list of paths) and on a media source; STRICT for the whole pass. A required path missing, an empty required media source, or — under STRICT — an unreadable file fails the pass with SourceMissingError, named in the FAILED message. New check offsite_backup.E009 under check --deploy: a required CONFIG path missing where it runs. Settings.

The guard without a cache. GUARD['BACKEND']: 'database' claims the night with a PostgreSQL session advisory lock on GUARD['DATABASE'], and reads "done" from the store. 'cache' stays the default. Scheduling.

Retries. The nightly task retries: Celery autoretry_for=(Exception,), max_retries=3, exponential backoff from a minute; taskiq register(broker, retries=3) puts retry_on_error/max_retries labels on it, for SimpleRetryMiddleware. A retry re-enters through the guard. The morning check is not retried. Scheduling.

The morning check and new databases. A database with no backup at all, beside databases that are backed up, is logged as "not backed up yet" instead of reported MISSING — a tenant created after the nightly pass. Stale backups, and the only database with none, are still MISSING. Monitoring.

Restore. restore_database(..., identity_text=...) takes a private key's text, for a dedicated identity the server holds on purpose; written to a private 0600 file and removed afterwards. Passing a file and text together is refused. Restore.

Documentation. A machine with only the recipient set is off; Celery beat entries follow CELERY_TIMEZONE; the deployment mount on the deploy's service and the worker; restoring a custom-format dump under a legacy .sql… name; mixed suffixes after switching formats; heartbeats of the two scheduled tasks; new rules on AI assistants.

docs.title: 0.1.0 — 2026-11-03
docs.text:
The first release.

A pass. manage.py backup_offsite (and offsite_backup.run()) backs up the databases, the media and the deployment configuration, one part at a time, then rotates. A database that fails does not cost the others their night; the pass fails at the end naming every one. --without-media and --only for partial passes; --reason for the message.

Databases. offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource: one alias, a list, or a callable that computes them at run time; plain SQL (.sql.zst.age) or the custom format (.dump.zst.age, pg_dump's compression off, then zstd). The password travels in PGPASSWORD, never on a command line. back_up_database() for a one-off dump with extra recipients, and keep_apart to set one aside from rotation.

Media. offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource and offsite_backup.media.s3.S3Source: volumes of whole files (4 GiB by default), each a complete tar written with Python's tarfile, streamed one at a time; INCLUDE/EXCLUDE globs; several sources.

Configuration. offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource: listed paths plus the environment rebuilt from a list of names, written last.

Encryption. offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli: compress, then encrypt, to one or more public keys, under pipefail semantics.

Stores. offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store: every upload locked COMPLIANCE by its own arguments and read back; multipart in 64 MiB parts; versions and delete markers handled; pagination everywhere; only the configured credentials. offsite_backup.stores.filesystem.DirectoryStore: atomic writes, 0600 files, and a warning that it has no immutability.

Retention. Whole UTC nights read from object names, per kind; passes without media never count as nights; every version deleted; locked versions left for a later night; depth in the message.

Messages. One HTML format for written, failed, missing and unchecked, every value escaped. Notifiers: LogNotifier, TelegramNotifier ([telegram], httpx2), TopicNotifier through django-aiogram ([aiogram]). A notifier never costs the backup.

Scheduling. run_nightly() with a once-per-night guard in a shared cache; Celery (offsite_backup.schedule.celery.beat_schedule) and taskiq (offsite_backup.schedule.taskiq.register) adapters.

Monitoring. manage.py backup_check — the morning check over the configuration folder and every database's; LAST_SUCCESS_FILE; manage.py backup_list.

Restore. manage.py backup_restore: download, decrypt and verify every object of a stamp; --apply loads a database (--from-database, --clean); restore_database().

System checks. E001–E008, W001–W005; network checks under check --deploy only.

Testing. A pytest plugin and OffsiteBackupTestRunner that silence network notifiers; capture(), FakeS3, use_fake_s3, Passthrough, media_tree.

docs.title: Configuration archive
docs.text:
'CONFIG': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource',
    'PATHS': ['/app/deploy'],
    'RENDER_ENV': 'deploy-vars.txt',
},

What it takes to rebuild the machine rather than the data: the compose file, the Dockerfile, the reverse-proxy configuration, certificates, signing keys — and the environment the deploy gave the application. One archive, tar | zstd | age, written last in every pass.

docs.title: Why last
docs.text: A configuration object for a stamp means every part before it went up. The morning check relies on that: it reads the config/ folder (and every database's) for the newest whole backup, so a pass that died half way cannot pass for a night.

docs.title: PATHS
docs.text:
Files and directories. A directory is archived under its own name, recursively; a file at the archive's root:

PATHS = ['/app/deploy', '/etc/acme/signing.pem']

deploy/compose.yml
deploy/Caddyfile
deploy/certs/node.pem
signing.pem
rendered.env

Inside a directory, symbolic links are skipped; files this process cannot read are skipped wherever they are. Files whose name matches .env or a glob in EXCLUDE are left out. EXCLUDE adds to .env, never replaces it: the live environment file does not travel whatever the list says.

A path that does not exist is left out, and the pass logs it (Configuration path not found; left out); manage.py check --deploy in that container says W005 — almost always a mount missing from one of the containers that run a pass. A plain manage.py check or migrate says nothing: the web service has no reason to mount it. Blank items are dropped, so os.environ.get('X', '') in the list is harmless where X is unset.

docs.title: Required paths
docs.text:
By default a missing path is left out, logged, and the pass goes on. When the certificates or signing keys are part of what restores the machine, a pass without them is not a whole backup — make them required:

'CONFIG': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource',
    'PATHS': ['/app/deploy', '/etc/acme/signing.pem'],
    'REQUIRED': ['/etc/acme/signing.pem'],   # or True: every path in PATHS
},
  • A required path missing at pass time fails the pass with SourceMissingError, and the FAILED message names it. The databases and media written before it stay written; the configuration archive — and so the night, for the morning check — does not.
  • manage.py check --deploy reports it as E009 in the container it runs in. A plain manage.py check does not: it runs in every container, most of which never run a pass, and an error there would stop migrate (why).
  • STRICT: True at the top level makes every path required, and a file that cannot be read fails the pass instead of being skipped (Settings).

Use REQUIRED for what a restore cannot do without; leave paths that may legitimately be absent on some machines optional.

docs.title: The live .env does not travel; a rebuilt one does
docs.text:
The live environment file is often unreadable to the application (another owner, a read-only mount), and copying it opportunistically would carry whatever else it holds. Its values already reached this process through the environment; what is missing is the list of names. Give that list in RENDER_ENV:

# deploy-vars.txt — one name per line, comments allowed
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
DATABASE_URL
BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY
BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY
SENTRY_DSN   # optional in staging

and the archive gets rendered.env at its root, rebuilt from the running process:

# Rebuilt from the running process, not copied. Names from deploy-vars.txt.
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY='s3cr3t$with spaces'
DATABASE_URL=postgres://acme:pw@db:5432/acme
BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY=AKIA...
BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY=...
# SENTRY_DSN was not set
  • A name that is not set is written down as such: "this deployment ran without it" is what a restore needs to know.
  • Values are quoted so that Docker Compose and a POSIX shell read back the same text. Plain values stay bare, anything else is single-quoted, and a value holding a single quote is double-quoted with \, ", $ and ` escaped.
  • A value holding a newline is not written — it would become extra lines, and a secret holding one could forge settings nobody set. A comment says it was skipped.

RENDER_ENV is relative to settings.BASE_DIR unless absolute. If your deploy renders the .env from a list of variable names already, point RENDER_ENV at that same list.

The archive therefore holds every secret the application has. It is sealed to your age recipient like everything else; whoever holds the private key holds all of it.

docs.title: Mount the deployment directory read-only — everywhere a pass runs
docs.text:
services:
  web:
    volumes:
      - ./:/app/deploy:ro
  worker:
    volumes:
      - ./:/app/deploy:ro

The worker runs the nightly pass; the deploy pass runs in the service your deploy starts it in (often the web image as a one-off). Both need the mount, or one of them archives an empty folder — the pass logs Configuration path not found; left out, and check --deploy in that service says W005 — or, for a required path, the pass fails and check --deploy says E009.

docs.title: Without CONFIG
docs.text: Leave it out and the morning check reads the databases' folders alone. A project with neither CONFIG nor DATABASES is checked on its media folders.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
'DATABASES': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource',
    'ALIASES': ['default'],
    'FORMAT': 'plain',
},

Three sources, one per engine — each a BACKEND of its own:

engine backend dumps with object suffix PostgreSQL offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource pg_dump .sql.zst.age / .dump.zst.age MySQL, MariaDB offsite_backup.databases.mysql.MySQLSource mysqldump / mariadb-dump --single-transaction .sql.zst.age SQLite offsite_backup.databases.sqlite.SQLiteSource Python's online backup API .sqlite3.zst.age

For each alias: dump | zstd | age into one file in the workspace, upload, delete, next. Nothing goes through Python memory. Most of this page is PostgreSQL's; what differs for the others is under MySQL and MariaDB and SQLite.

docs.title: Which databases
docs.text:
ALIASES names entries of Django's DATABASES:

OneSeveralComputed at run time 
'DATABASES': {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource'},

ALIASES defaults to ['default'].

'DATABASES': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource',
    'ALIASES': ['default', 'analytics'],
},

'DATABASES': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource',
    'ALIASES': 'acme.tenancy.backup_aliases',
},

A dotted path to a callable that takes no arguments and returns the aliases — for a project that adds a database per tenant. It is called at the start of every pass and of every morning check. Aliases added to connections.databases at run time count.

Each alias is its own kind: db/ for default, db-<alias>/ for every other — a sibling, not a child, or db/'s rotation would count it. Each kind rotates by itself.

One database that cannot be dumped does not cost the others — nor the media, nor the configuration — their night. The pass goes on, uploads the rest, rotates, and then fails naming every alias that did not go up:

backup_offsite: 1 database(s) not backed up, the rest went up — analytics: PipelineError: `pg_dump` exited with status 1: ...

docs.title: The connection
docs.text:
From DATABASES[alias] — or, when the source has a CONNECTIONS block, from that block's CONNECTIONS[alias], with the same keys. CONNECTIONS is how a server with no Django project names its databases (Without Django), and how a Django project names one it does not want in DATABASES:

'DATABASES': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource',
    'ALIASES': ['default'],
    'CONNECTIONS': {
        'default': {'HOST': 'db', 'PORT': '5432', 'USER': 'app', 'PASSWORD': os.environ.get('DB_PASSWORD', ''), 'NAME': 'app'},
    },
},

With CONNECTIONS set, Django's DATABASES is not read at all for this source, and an alias missing from it is refused by name. ALIASES still says which are dumped.

HOST, PORT, USER and NAME become pg_dump flags; PASSWORD travels in PGPASSWORD, never on the command line — a command line is visible in ps, and an error text is posted to a chat. OPTIONS['sslmode'] and OPTIONS['sslrootcert'] become PGSSLMODE and PGSSLROOTCERT. The connection shows up in pg_stat_activity as application_name = offsite_backup. Every question the package asks the server — whether a restore target is empty, how many rows a table holds, the server's version for E004 — goes through psql with the same connection, so it needs no Django connection either.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
FORMAT pg_dump object suffix restored with plain (default) plain SQL .sql.zst.age psql --single-transaction custom --format=custom --compress=0 .dump.zst.age pg_restore --single-transaction

The suffix names the format. A custom-format archive under a .sql. name gets fed to psql in a hurry, and fails. A restore does not trust the name anyway: it tells the formats apart by the archive's magic bytes (PGDMP), and decompresses whatever starts with zstd's — so objects written under an older naming scheme restore too.

Switching from custom-format dumps named .sql…. A project whose own backups were custom-format dumps under a .sql.zst.age name, and which now sets FORMAT: 'custom', sees both names in a database's folder for one retention window — the old .sql.zst.age objects, the new .dump.zst.age ones — until the old ones rotate out. That is expected and harmless: rotation reads nights from the stamps, not from the suffix, and a restore detects the format from the magic bytes. There is no option to keep the old suffix: a suffix that does not name the format is how a custom dump ends up fed to psql.

The custom format is dumped with pg_dump's own compression off and compressed by zstd: zstd compresses better, and compressed data does not compress twice. It is what you want when you need pg_restore --list (an integrity read of the whole table of contents, which backup_restore runs) or to restore one table from a dump. Plain SQL is readable with zstd -dc | less and loads into anything that speaks SQL.

By default both carry --no-owner --no-privileges, so a dump restores into a database owned by a different role. NO_OWNER: False keeps ownership and grants. EXTRA_ARGS is appended to the command — ['--exclude-table-data=django_session'], for example.

docs.title: How a dump is known to be whole
docs.text:
The pipeline runs with pipefail semantics and no shell: every stage's exit status is read, so a pg_dump that dies half way fails the pass instead of leaving a small, valid, truncated .age. The tail of the failing stage's stderr goes into the error.

A restore checks again: a plain dump must end with PostgreSQL database dump complete; a custom one must pass pg_restore --list.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
pg_dump refuses to dump a server newer than itself. python manage.py check --deploy connects to each alias and compares:

?: (offsite_backup.E004) pg_dump is 16, older than the server of 'default' (18).
    HINT: Install the PostgreSQL 18 client (e.g. postgresql-client-18) in the image.

An alias it cannot connect to is skipped by this check rather than reported.

docs.title: A one-off backup of one database
docs.text:
For the moment a database is about to go — removed, put to sleep, handed back:

from offsite_backup import back_up_database

key = back_up_database('tenant_42')

It raises when backups are not configured, so a removal that cannot be backed up does not happen. The dump goes to <PREFIX>/db-tenant_42/ like a nightly one; nothing rotates that folder once the alias is no longer among the pass's targets.

  • extra_recipients=['age1...'] seals this one dump to more keys as well — for a database the server itself must be able to restore later (waking a tenant), seal it to a key the server holds. Every other backup stays readable off the machine only. Restoring it on the server: restore_database(..., identity_text=...) (Restore).
  • keep_apart=True writes it under <PREFIX>/released/db-<alias>/ instead, where no rotation ever reads — so an alias reused later never mixes two databases' history.

keep_apart(key) does the same for a backup already stored: it copies the object under <PREFIX>/released/, locked afresh, and answers the new key. The original stays where its own rotation will take it.

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text: backup_restore --apply and restore_database() — see Restore.

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text:
'DATABASES': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.mysql.MySQLSource',
    'ALIASES': ['default'],
    'CLIENT': 'mariadb',   # 'mysql' (default): mysqldump and mysql
},

ALIASES works as for PostgreSQL. Each dump is

mysqldump --defaults-extra-file=<0600 file> --single-transaction --quick --hex-blob --triggers
          --no-tablespaces --default-character-set=utf8mb4 [--set-gtid-purged=OFF] <EXTRA_ARGS> <NAME>
  • One moment of the database. --single-transaction reads every InnoDB table as of the dump's start, without locking a table against the application. A MyISAM table is not covered by it — it is read as it is while the dump runs; convert it, or accept that.
  • The password never reaches argv, nor MYSQL_PWD (deprecated by MySQL): HOST (a path starting with / is a socket), PORT, USER, PASSWORD, OPTIONS['unix_socket'] and OPTIONS['ssl'] go into an option file readable by this process only, passed as --defaults-extra-file and removed when the dump ends.
  • --set-gtid-purged=OFF (MySQL only, which mariadb-dump does not know): a dump carrying the server's GTID set refuses to load into any other server.
  • --no-tablespaces spares the dump user the PROCESS privilege. Routines and events are not dumped by default — Django does not create them; 'EXTRA_ARGS': ['--routines', '--events'] adds them for a project that does.
  • Whole: a restore checks the dump ends with -- Dump completed, the line both programs write last (so do not pass --skip-comments).
  • No Python driver needed: the source runs only the client programs. A restore asks the server through mysql / mariadb whether the target holds any table, refuses one that does unless --clean — which drops every table and view first, foreign key checks off — then feeds the dump to the client, which stops at the first error.

The client should be at least as new as the server: mysql-client for MySQL, mariadb-client for MariaDB (mysqldump 8 against a MariaDB server trips on statistics tables MariaDB does not have).

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
'DATABASES': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.sqlite.SQLiteSource',
    'ALIASES': ['default'],
},

Each alias's NAME is a file. It is copied with sqlite3.Connection.backup — the online backup API — into the pass's private workspace, then compressed and sealed from there and the copy removed. The backup API copies page by page and starts over when a writer touches a page it has copied, so the copy is one moment of the database while the application keeps writing; copying the file itself could catch a transaction half way, or miss what only the write-ahead log (-wal) holds. No binary is needed.

  • The workspace holds one plain copy of the database for the length of its sealing — mind WORKDIR on a machine whose temporary directory is small or shared.
  • A database file that does not exist fails that database (SourceMissingError) instead of creating an empty one; check --deploy reports it as W005, or E009 with 'REQUIRED': True. An alias that is not SQLite, or an in-memory database, is E001.
  • Verified on restore: an SQLite header and PRAGMA integrity_check answering ok.
  • Restored with the same backup API over the target alias's file, which must hold no table unless --clean. Close the application's connections to it first.

docs.title: Other databases
docs.text: A subclass of offsite_backup.databases.base.DatabaseSource named in BACKEND works without any change to the package: targets() (the ALIASES logic is the base class's), suffix(), dump(), verify() and restore().

docs.title: Deploy integration
docs.text:
A migration changes the database; the backup that matters most is the one taken just before it. Put one command in front of your migrations:

The deploy line

python manage.py backup_offsite --without-media --reason deploy

Both flags, every time. --reason deploy is what makes a failure say "The deploy stops here"; without it the pass reads DEFAULT_REASON — manual unless you set it, "✋ By hand" in the chat.

  • It runs on the new image, before migrate.
  • Non-zero stops the deploy. The old release keeps serving, and the chat says "The deploy stops here; the live release keeps serving."
  • It writes the databases and the configuration, not the media: a migration changes the database, never the media, and the media is what makes a pass long — measured, a whole pass with 5.2 GB of media took 1044 s, and a deploy waited for it. The media goes up every night anyway.
  • Its objects carry the .without-media. marker (where MEDIA is configured), so a deploy at noon never counts as a night: it cannot push a whole night out of retention, and it cannot hide a night that never ran from the morning check.
  • On a machine where backups are off it prints "nothing to do" and exits 0, so the same pipeline deploys a staging machine that has no keys.

Forgetting --reason. backup_offsite defaults to --reason manual: a person running it by hand is the common case. A deploy step that leaves the flag out is read as a pass by hand, and its failure message lacks the deploy line. As a safeguard, --without-media without an explicit --reason prints a one-line notice to stderr:

backup_offsite: the reason is 'manual'; before a deploy, pass --reason deploy (the message then says the deploy stops on failure)

A project that only ever runs the command from its deploy may set the default instead:

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {..., 'DEFAULT_REASON': 'deploy'}

An explicit --reason always wins, and prints no notice.

docs.title: Where it runs, and what it needs there
docs.text:
Run it where the new release's settings and image are, not the old one's: a deploy that adds a notifier token, a database or a binary should have its own pre-deploy pass use them. The service it runs in needs:

  • the backup's environment variables (store, recipient, notifier);
  • a connection to the database;
  • the deployment directory, mounted read-only, for the configuration archive — in this service and in the worker that runs the nightly pass. Both run a pass, and each archives what its container sees: a mount on one of them only gives the other an empty (or failing, with REQUIRED) configuration archive.
services:
  web:
    image: registry.example.com/acme/web:${TAG}
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      - ./:/app/deploy:ro
  worker:
    image: registry.example.com/acme/web:${TAG}
    command: celery -A acme worker
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      - ./:/app/deploy:ro

Here web is the service the deploy runs the pass in (docker compose run --rm web ..., below) and worker runs the nightly pass. manage.py check --deploy names a path missing in the container it runs in: W005, or E009 for a REQUIRED one. A plain manage.py check and migrate say nothing about paths, so a container without the mount deploys quietly; in the worker, which runs no system check, the pass logs what it left out.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
set -euo pipefail
export TAG=1.42.0
docker compose pull
docker compose run --rm --no-deps web python manage.py backup_offsite --without-media --reason deploy
docker compose run --rm --no-deps web python manage.py migrate --no-input
docker compose up -d

run --rm --no-deps starts a one-off container of the new image without restarting anything; set -e stops the script — and the deploy — on a failed backup.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - name: Deploy
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }}

            docker compose run --rm --no-deps web python manage.py migrate --no-input
            docker compose up -d

docs.title: Kubernetes, Helm, and the rest
docs.text: The same command as a pre-upgrade hook or an init step that runs before the migration Job, with restartPolicy: Never and backoffLimit: 0: a failed backup must fail the release, not retry until it happens to pass.

docs.title: Before the first deploy
docs.text:
• Run python manage.py check --deploy in the new image as part of your pipeline's test or build stage, against production settings if you can: E004 (a pg_dump older than the server) and E005/E006 (a bucket without Object Lock or its default rule) are better found there than at the deploy. Run it once in the service the deploy runs the pass in, with the mount, for E009 and W005 (a required or an optional path missing there).
  • Make sure the CI job that runs your tests does not inherit the production notifier token — see Testing.
  • Run the deploy pass once by hand and restore it (Restore).

docs.title: Encryption and keys
docs.text:
'ENCRYPTION': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
    'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
},

Every object is encrypted with age to one or more public keys. The server holds only public keys, so it can write a backup and cannot read one. The private half lives off the machine — in your password manager, and nowhere else.

docs.title: Making a key pair
docs.text:
On your own machine, not the server:

age-keygen -o backup-acme-prod.key
# Public key: age1qyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqs3290gq
  • The public key (age1…) goes into the server's environment, e.g. BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT. It is not a secret.
  • The file holds the private key (AGE-SECRET-KEY-1…). Put it in your password manager, then delete the file. age-keygen -y backup-acme-prod.key prints the public key again from it.

One key pair per product and environment keeps a leaked key's reach small. Losing the private key loses every backup sealed to it — store it where at least two people can reach it.

docs.title: RECIPIENTS
docs.text:
One public key, a list, or one string holding several. A string is split on commas and newlines, and between age1… keys on whitespace too — an ssh-ed25519 … recipient keeps the space inside it. Blank items are dropped, so the environment idiom works as it is:

'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENTS', ''),   # 'age1abc..., age1def...'

On a machine where the variable is unset this is '' — and a list of blanks, [os.environ.get('X', '')], counts as unset too: with the store credentials present, E001 names RECIPIENTS (Settings).

With several recipients, any one of the private keys opens a backup — a second key for a colleague, or a break-glass key in a safe.

age's SSH recipients (ssh-ed25519 …, ssh-rsa …) are accepted too.

manage.py check refuses anything else in RECIPIENTS as E008 — above all a private key, which would put the means to read every backup on the machine they protect:

?: (offsite_backup.E008) OFFSITE_BACKUP['ENCRYPTION']['RECIPIENTS'] holds a PRIVATE age key.
    HINT: Put the public half (age1...) here; the private half belongs off this machine.

docs.title: Compress, then encrypt
docs.text:
The order is not a preference: an encrypted stream does not compress. Databases and the configuration archive go source | zstd | age; media volumes go tar | age, because images and video are compressed already.

'COMPRESS': ['zstd', '-19', '--long=27', '-T0', '-q'],   # the default
'DECOMPRESS': ['zstd', '-d', '-q', '--long=31'],         # what a restore runs

-19 --long=27 is slow and small, which suits a batch job at night. A large database that does not finish in its window is better served by -10 than by no compression; an empty COMPRESS turns the stage off. DECOMPRESS must accept the window COMPRESS used — --long=31 accepts any. A restore decides whether to decompress from zstd's magic bytes, not from the name.

Every stage runs under pipefail semantics: a stage that dies mid-stream fails the pass instead of leaving a small, valid, truncated file.

docs.title: A second key for one dump: the wake identity
docs.text:
Some databases must be restorable by the server itself — a tenant put to sleep and woken on demand. Seal that one dump to an extra recipient whose private key the server holds, and keep every other backup readable off the machine only:

from offsite_backup import back_up_database, restore_database

key = back_up_database('tenant_42', extra_recipients=[settings.WAKE_RECIPIENT])
...
restore_database(key, 'tenant_42', identity=settings.WAKE_IDENTITY_FILE)
# or, with the key's text rather than a file:
restore_database(key, 'tenant_42', identity_text=settings.WAKE_IDENTITY)

identity_text is written to a private 0600 temporary file and removed afterwards. It is for this dedicated, narrowly used identity only — never the backups' main key.

The server's wake key opens those dumps and nothing else. Treat it as a secret of the server, with the same care as its database password.

docs.title: Without the binary: pyrage
docs.text:
'ENCRYPTION': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.pyrage.Pyrage',
    'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENTS', ''),
},

pip install 'django-offsite-backup[pyrage]' — pyrage is age's Rust implementation in a wheel, for an image where installing the age binary is the hard part. It is the same format: a backup sealed by Pyrage opens with age -d, and one sealed by age opens with Pyrage — CI seals with each and opens with the other. So switching between the two needs no re-encryption, and a restore on your own machine can use whichever is installed there.

RECIPIENTS, E008 and the extra recipients work exactly as for AgeCli; a recipient pyrage itself cannot read is E008 as well. Identity files are age's: AGE-SECRET-KEY-1… lines (comments allowed), or one SSH private key.

A pipeline stage is a process, so each sealing stage is this interpreter running python -m offsite_backup.encryption.pyrage seal age1… (or open <identity file> on restore), streaming stdin to stdout through pyrage.encrypt_io / decrypt_io — memory stays flat whatever the size, and the stage fails the pass like any other under pipefail. Recipients are public keys and the identity is a file path, so argv holds no secret. Where sys.executable is not Python — inside uWSGI — set 'PYTHON': '/usr/local/bin/python'.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: An explicit "no encryption" backend and helpers to re-seal recent backups to a new recipient are on the roadmap. For tests, offsite_backup.testing.Passthrough stands in for age — and raises W002 so it is never mistaken for encryption (Testing).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
S3 + TelegramS3 + django-aiogramDirectory onlyA server without Django 
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[s3,telegram]'

Backups in an S3 bucket with Object Lock, messages through the Telegram Bot API.

pip install 'django-offsite-backup[s3,aiogram]'

Messages through the bot your project already runs with django-aiogram; no token in these settings.

pip install django-offsite-backup

A local directory or Docker volume as the store, messages to the log. No driver at all — and no immutability either; see Stores: directory.

pipx install 'django-offsite-backup[cli,s3,telegram]'

The offsite-backup command, a TOML setting, the same passes — see Without Django.

Requires Python 3.10–3.14, and Django 5.2+ for the Django layer (a Django project has it already). Every pair in that range runs in CI, and an integration job runs a whole cycle — backup, restore into a clean database, row counts of every table compared — against PostgreSQL 16 and 18 and an S3 server with Object Lock, and another against MySQL 8.4 and MariaDB 11.4.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
The base install pulls nothing — not even Django, which a Django project brings itself and a plain server does not need. Every backend is named by a dotted path in the settings, imported only when a pass first needs it, and its driver is an extra:

extra pulls for django django>=5.2 the Django layer — the app, the commands, the system checks — where the project does not already pin Django cli tomli>=2.0 on Python 3.10 only the offsite-backup command's TOML setting (Without Django) s3 boto3>=1.34 offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store, offsite_backup.media.s3.S3Source telegram httpx2>=2.0 offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier webhook httpx2>=2.0 offsite_backup.notifiers.webhook.WebhookNotifier aiogram django-aiogram>=5.2 offsite_backup.notifiers.django_aiogram.TopicNotifier pyrage pyrage>=1.2.3 offsite_backup.encryption.pyrage.Pyrage — age without the age binary all all of the above

The MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, Docker-volume and Django-storage backends need no extra: the first two run the database's own client or the standard library, the Docker one the docker CLI, and a Django storage brings its own package (django-storages and its driver).

Nothing is inferred from what happens to be installed. When a configured backend's driver is missing, manage.py check says so with the install line (E002):

?: (offsite_backup.E002) OFFSITE_BACKUP['STORE']['BACKEND'] is S3Store, but its driver is not installed.
    HINT: pip install "django-offsite-backup[s3]"

docs.title: Binaries
docs.text:
A pass streams through command-line tools rather than through Python memory. They are not Python dependencies; install them in the image that runs the backup:

binary needed for checked by pg_dump PostgresSource — its major version must be at least the server's E003, and E004 under check --deploy zstd COMPRESS (on by default) and DECOMPRESS (restoring) — whatever program they name E003 age AgeCli, both for sealing and for restoring — not needed with Pyrage E003 psql, pg_restore restoring a database (backup_restore --apply, the drill), verifying a custom-format dump, and every question asked of the server (is the target empty, row counts, its version); shipped with pg_dump in every PostgreSQL client package E003 mysqldump, mysql — or mariadb-dump, mariadb MySQLSource, by its CLIENT: dumping, restoring, and the drill's questions (is the target empty, row counts) E003 docker VolumeSource, with the daemon's socket E003, and E012 under check --deploy

tar is not needed: volumes and the configuration archive are written with Python's tarfile. Measured on 613 MB in 2400 files, tarfile took 0.27 s against 0.72 s for the tar CLI, and it is the only option for media streamed from S3, which has no files on disk to hand to tar.

On Debian-based images:

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends age zstd postgresql-common \
 && /usr/share/postgresql-common/pgdg/apt.postgresql.org.sh -y \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends postgresql-client-18 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Match postgresql-client-<N> to your server's major version, or newer: pg_dump refuses to dump a server newer than itself.

docs.title: Add the app
docs.text:
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    'offsite_backup',
]

The app registers the system checks and imports nothing else: no backend, no driver, no network until a pass runs. It has no models and no migrations.

docs.title: A first pass
docs.text:
1. Make a key pair on your machine, not the server, and keep the private half in your password manager (Encryption):

    age-keygen -o backup-acme-prod.key
# Public key: age1...

  2. Create the bucket with Object Lock, and a default COMPLIANCE rule of 13 days (S3 providers).

  3. Put the settings in settings.py, reading every credential from the environment (Settings):

    import os

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {
    'PREFIX': 'acme/prod',
    'ENV': 'prod',
    'STORE': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
        'ENDPOINT_URL': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT', ''),
        'REGION': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_REGION', ''),
        'BUCKET': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_BUCKET', ''),
        'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
        'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
    },
    'ENCRYPTION': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
        'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
    },
    'DATABASES': {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource'},
    'CONFIG': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource',
        'PATHS': ['/app/deploy'],
    },
    'NOTIFY': [
        {
            'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier',
            'TOKEN': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN', ''),
            'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
        },
    ],
}

  4. Check, then run:

    python manage.py check
python manage.py check --deploy      # reaches the bucket and the database; the mounts a pass reads
python manage.py backup_offsite
# backup_offsite: 2 objects, 18734112 bytes up

  5. Restore it once, now, before you need to — Restore.

Then schedule the nightly pass and the morning check (Scheduling) and put the deploy pass in front of your migrations (Deploy integration).

docs.title: Media
docs.text:
'MEDIA': [
    {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource'},
],

Uploaded files, whatever holds them, packed into volumes of whole files.

docs.title: Where the media lives
Volumes
docs.text:
Media goes up in volumes of at most VOLUME_BYTES (4 GiB by default):

acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.tar.age
acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.002.tar.age
acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.003.tar.age
  • Whole files only. Each volume is a complete tar on its own: losing one loses its files, not the night, and any one of them restores with tar -x.
  • A file larger than a volume gets a volume of its own.
  • The budget counts tar's overhead: 20 KiB per volume (the end-of-archive blocks and the padding to a record) and 2 KiB per file (a 512-byte header, padding to 512, and a PAX header for a long or non-ASCII name), so a volume of many small files stays under the limit.
  • Streamed, one at a time: source → tar → age → disk → upload → delete, then the next volume — packed while the files stream, so a source is listed (or, for a Docker volume, read) once. The workspace needs room for one sealed volume, not for the media; media larger than the free disk works.
  • Why 4 GiB: one S3 PUT stops at 5 GB. Volumes above 64 MiB go up multipart anyway, but a volume small enough for one PUT is the one that never surprises anyone. VOLUME_BYTES must be more than 20 KiB and at most 5 GB (E001).

Volumes are written with Python's tarfile in PAX format — measured faster than the tar CLI (0.27 s against 0.72 s on 613 MB in 2400 files), and the only option when the files come from S3. Each member is written with mode 0644 and the file's modification time; the size is taken when the file is opened, so a file that changed since it was listed is archived as it is now.

Not compressed by default. Images, video and PDFs are already compressed; zstd would spend the night gaining nothing. COMPRESS: True on a source runs the global COMPRESS stage on its volumes as well, and the suffix becomes .tar.zst.age.

docs.title: Manifests
docs.text:
Every volume has a manifest beside it, sealed like the volume (not compressed):

acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.tar.age
acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.manifest.json.age

{"format": 1, "volume": "2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.tar.age",
 "files": [{"path": "invoices/2026/03/0001.pdf", "size": 48213, "sha256": "9f2c…"}]}

Each file's path, size and SHA-256 are taken while it streams into the tar — the bytes written, not the size listed. A restore of one file or one folder (backup_restore --path, Restore) downloads the manifests, then only the volumes that hold a match, and checks every file against its hash. A manifest goes up right after its volume, rotates with it (its night is in its name), and is counted among the pass's objects. File names can be as telling as the files, so a manifest is encrypted to the same recipients.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
INCLUDE and EXCLUDE are lists of shell globs matched against each file's name inside the archive (fnmatch: * matches across / too); blank items are dropped. With INCLUDE, only matching names are kept; then anything matching EXCLUDE is left out:

'EXCLUDE': ['*.tmp', 'cache/*', '*/thumbs/*'],   # regenerable, not worth a night's upload

For S3Source the name includes PREFIX — write 'private/media/cache/*', or narrow PREFIX instead.

docs.title: Several sources
docs.text:
MEDIA is a list. Each source is a kind of its own, with its own volumes and its own rotation; give each a NAME:

'MEDIA': [
    {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource', 'ROOT': '/app/media'},
    {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource', 'ROOT': '/app/private', 'NAME': 'private'},
],

acme/prod/media/...
acme/prod/media-private/...

A single block instead of a list is accepted too.

docs.title: Empty is not an error — unless it is required
docs.text:
A source with no files writes no volume, and the message says how many objects went up. The morning check does not depend on media: tonight's media does not stand in for a database that was not written.

When an empty source can only mean a missing mount or a wrong ROOT / PREFIX, make it required: 'REQUIRED': True on the source (or STRICT: True for the whole pass) turns "no files at all" into a failed pass, with SourceMissingError naming the source in the FAILED message (Settings).

docs.title: Leaving media out of one pass
docs.text: backup_offsite --without-media (or --only db --only config) writes the databases and the configuration only, and — in a project that has MEDIA configured — marks every object .without-media.: the pass a deploy runs. Those objects never count as a night; see Retention and Deploy integration.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: A failed pass says so. The night that never ran — the scheduler stopped, the worker was never deployed, the machine was off — says nothing at all. The morning check is the answer to that silence.

docs.title: The morning check
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_check
# backup_check: ok, newest whole backup 2026-03-10 03:00 UTC

It asks the store for the newest whole backup under:

  • the config/ folder, when CONFIG is set, and
  • every database's folder — db/, db-<alias>/ for each alias the pass would dump today,
  • or, with neither configured, every media folder.

Objects marked .without-media. do not count: a deploy at noon cannot stand in for a night that never ran. Media does not count either while there are databases or a configuration: tonight's media does not stand in for a database that was not written.

finding message exit every folder has a whole backup within STALE_HOURS (26) none 0 a database with no backup at all, beside databases that are backed up none — logged at INFO, Databases not backed up yet (below) 0 some folder's newest is older, or there is none MISSING, naming the oldest non-zero (BackupMissingError) the store could not be read UNCHECKED — as loud as missing non-zero (BackupUncheckedError) backups are off on this machine none 0, "nothing to do"

The error names every stale folder:

CommandError: backup_check: No whole backup within 26 h under acme/prod/: db-analytics/ (none), config/ (2026-03-08 03:00 UTC)

STALE_HOURS is 26 so that a pass at 03:00 one night and a slow one the next still pass a check at 09:00. Raise it if your nightly pass runs less often than daily.

docs.title: A database added today
docs.text:
With ALIASES a callable, the list of databases is computed at every check — and a tenant created after the nightly pass has no backup at all at the morning check. That is not a missed night, so:

  • a database folder with no backup at all, beside databases that are backed up, is "not backed up yet": logged at INFO (Databases not backed up yet, the kinds in ob_kinds), not MISSING. Its first nightly pass backs it up;
  • a database whose backups exist but are stale is MISSING, as before;
  • the only database, with no backup at all, is still MISSING — there is nothing beside it to show that the passes run;
  • a database whose dump fails every night is not silent either: each night's FAILED message names it.

Schedule it as in Scheduling; from Python it is offsite_backup.check_last_night(), which returns the oldest of the newest whole backups (or None where backups are off) and raises the same errors.

docs.title: The last-success file
docs.text:
'LAST_SUCCESS_FILE': '/var/run/acme/backup-last-success',

After every successful pass the file is rewritten with the pass's time in ISO format:

2026-03-10T03:00:12.402113+00:00

Something already watching the machine can read its age — a node-exporter textfile collector, a Docker healthcheck, a monitoring agent's file-age check. It is written by every successful pass, deploy passes and passes by hand included, so it answers "did anything succeed lately", not "did last night run"; the morning check — or backup_status, per kind — answers that. A file that cannot be written is logged (Last-success marker not written) and does not fail the pass. Mount the path where your monitor can see it — the worker writes it at night, the deploy's one-off container before a migration.

docs.title: The age of every kind
docs.text:
The morning check says MISSING once a day, in the chat. A monitor wants the same answer whenever it asks, silently, and as a number:

python manage.py backup_status                # or: offsite-backup status
# acme/prod/ (stale after 26 h)
#   config/: 2026-03-10 03:00 UTC, 6.2 h ago
#   db/: 2026-03-10 03:00 UTC, 6.2 h ago
#   media/: 2026-03-10 03:00 UTC, 6.2 h ago

For every kind — the config, every database the pass would dump today, and every media source — it reads the newest whole backup from the store, as the morning check does (objects of a pass without media do not count), and its age. Nothing is notified.

finding exit every kind has a whole backup within STALE_HOURS (or --stale-hours H) 0 a kind's newest is older, or there is none (STALE on its line) 1 the store could not be read 2 backups are off on this machine 0, "nothing to do"

That makes it a healthcheck as it is — a cron job's exit status, a Docker HEALTHCHECK, a monitoring agent's command check, a push to a dead man's switch on success. --json is for a script; from Python, offsite_backup.freshness() returns the same figures (kinds, each with kind, newest, seconds, stale) and raises BackupUncheckedError when the store cannot be read.

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_status --prometheus /var/lib/node_exporter/textfile/offsite_backup.prom

writes the text exposition format for node-exporter's textfile collector (or any scraper that reads a file) — atomically, so a scrape never reads half a file — and still exits as above. Run it from cron every few minutes, or after the pass:

offsite_backup_up{prefix="acme/prod"} 1
offsite_backup_checked_timestamp_seconds{prefix="acme/prod"} 1773133200
offsite_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds{prefix="acme/prod",kind="db"} 1773111600
offsite_backup_stale{prefix="acme/prod",kind="db"} 0
metric offsite_backup_up 1 when the store was read; 0 — and nothing else is written — when it was not offsite_backup_checked_timestamp_seconds when the store was asked offsite_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds{kind} when the newest whole backup of the kind was written; absent for a kind with none offsite_backup_stale{kind} 1 when the kind has no whole backup within the threshold

An alert, for example:

- alert: OffsiteBackupStale
  expr: offsite_backup_stale == 1 or offsite_backup_up == 0
  for: 30m
- alert: OffsiteBackupNotChecked
  expr: time() - offsite_backup_checked_timestamp_seconds > 3 * 3600

The second catches the textfile itself going stale — the job that writes it stopped.

docs.title: The log
docs.text:
Everything is logged to the offsite_backup logger, with fields in the record's extra (prefixed ob_, so a JSON formatter can keep them apart from your own):

level message fields INFO Backup written ob_prefix, ob_objects, ob_bytes INFO Database backed up (a one-off backup) ob_alias, ob_key INFO Nightly backup skipped: ... (off, done, or being done) — INFO Databases not backed up yet (the morning check) ob_kinds ERROR (with traceback) Database not backed up ob_alias ERROR (with traceback) Store not written; left out of this pass — one of several stores refused an object ob_store WARNING Backup still locked; left for a later night ob_key, ob_until WARNING Backup depth not read ob_folder WARNING Last-success marker not written ob_path, ob_error WARNING Media file not listed, Media file not readable; left out ob_path, ob_error WARNING Configuration path not found; left out, Media directory not found — a mount missing where the pass ran (W005 under check --deploy) ob_path INFO Restore drill passed ob_prefix, ob_stamp ERROR (with traceback) Database not restored by the drill, Archive not opened by the drill ob_key, ob_step ERROR (with traceback) Drill database not emptied ob_alias WARNING Live database not counted (the drill) ob_alias, ob_error (the class only) WARNING Media volume not found — a VolumeSource Docker volume that does not exist (W005 under check --deploy) ob_volume WARNING Media file is a hard link; left out — in a Docker volume ob_path ERROR Notifier not built, Notifier raised ob_notifier, ob_error ERROR Backup message not formatted ob_error ERROR Telegram refused the backup message ob_status, ob_description ERROR Telegram unreachable, Backup message not sent through the bot ob_error (the class only) ERROR Webhook refused or unreachable ob_status or ob_error (the class only), ob_attempts ERROR Webhook body not built ob_error INFO / ERROR Backup written / Backup failed ... from LogNotifier (INFO for a written backup and a passed drill) ob_prefix, ob_text

No message, token, password or private key is ever logged.

docs.title: Heartbeats of scheduled tasks
docs.text:
A project that tracks when each of its scheduled tasks last ran — a heartbeat table, a "last run" dashboard — sees the package's tasks as never run until each has run once: the nightly pass after its first 03:00, the check after its first 09:00, the drill after its first month. Register them under their task names, the same for Celery and taskiq:

task default schedule (UTC) offsite_backup.nightly 03:00 offsite_backup.check 09:00 offsite_backup.drill only when scheduled — e.g. the 1st of the month, 05:00 (Scheduling)

docs.title: What the store holds
docs.text: python manage.py backup_list prints, per kind, the nights kept, the oldest night, the objects and bytes, the newest stamp, how long the newest object is locked and how many objects came from passes without media. --json for scripts. See Restore.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
'NOTIFY': [
    {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier',
        'TOKEN': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN', ''),
        'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
        'TOPIC_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID', ''),
    },
],

Every outcome — written, failed, missing, unchecked, and a drill passed or failed — is said where a person reads it. NOTIFY is a list; every notifier in it gets every message.

docs.title: What the messages look like
docs.text:
HTML, written to be read on a phone among everything else in the chat: the first line is what happened and where, the second why it ran, figures one per line, hashtags last — so a thread of them is searchable by kind, and a failure never looks like the hundred successes around it.

WrittenFailedMissingUncheckedDrill passedDrill failed 
💾 Backup written: acme/prod
🌙 Nightly

📦 Objects: 7
⚖️ Size: 5312.4 MB
⏱ Took: 1044s
🗄 Kept: 14 days, since 2026-02-25
🧹 Past the window: 7 removed

#backup #prod #nightly #ok

Kept is left out when the depth could not be read; Past the window when nothing was removed. A pass without media adds 🖼 Media: left to the nightly pass.

🚨 Backup FAILED: acme/prod
🚀 Before a deploy
The deploy stops here; the live release keeps serving.

1 database(s) not backed up, the rest went up — default: PipelineError: `pg_dump` exited with status 1: pg_dump: error: aborting because of server version mismatch

#backup #prod #deploy #failed

The error is cut at 500 characters. The deploy line appears only for --reason deploy; --reason upgrade says instead The upgrade stops here; the running <NAME> keeps serving.

🚨 Backup MISSING: acme/prod
🕘 Morning check

Newest backup: 2026-03-09 03:00 UTC, 30 h ago
Expected within 26 h

#backup #prod #missing

🚨 Backups UNCHECKED: acme/prod
🕘 Morning check: the store could not be read

ClientError: An error occurred (InvalidAccessKeyId) ...

#backup #prod #missing

As loud as missing, on purpose: a check that could not look has not seen a backup.

🧪 Restore drill passed: acme/prod
📅 Backup of 2026-03-10T03-00Z, restored into drill

🗃 default: 46 tables, 69 535 rows (live: 46 tables, 69 600 rows)
🖼 media: 2 volumes, 12 034 files, 5312.4 MB
⚙️ config: 42 files, 0.4 MB
⏱ Took: 812s

#backup #prod #drill #ok

A line per database — the live figures only with COMPARE_LIVE — and per kind of archive. A table the live database has and the restore lacks adds ⚠️ Not in the backup, live now: public.new_table. Restore.

🚨 Restore drill FAILED: acme/prod
📅 Backup of 2026-03-10T03-00Z

1 part(s) of 2026-03-10T03-00Z did not come back — acme/prod/db-analytics/2026-03-10T03-00Z.sql.zst.age: restore into 'drill': PipelineError: `psql` exited with status 3: ...

🗃 default: 46 tables, 69 535 rows (live: 46 tables, 69 600 rows)

#backup #prod #drill #failed

Every object that did not come back is named with the step it failed at; what did come back is listed under it.

The second line comes from --reason:

reason line hashtag nightly 🌙 Nightly #nightly deploy 🚀 Before a deploy #deploy manual (the command's default, see DEFAULT_REASON), by hand ✋ By hand #manual upgrade ⬆️ Before an upgrade #upgrade anything else 🔁 Reason #reason, non-alphanumerics replaced by _

Every interpolated value is escaped. A chat rejects a message whose HTML does not parse, and an error text with a < in it would otherwise be lost silently.

docs.title: Telegram
docs.text:
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[telegram]' — the Bot API over HTTPS with httpx2.

option TOKEN, CHAT_ID required TOPIC_ID a forum topic (message_thread_id); None, empty or 0 for the main thread; not an integer is E010 TIMEOUT seconds, default 10 API_URL default https://api.telegram.org; for a local Bot API server
  • A topic id typed wrong makes Telegram refuse the message. It is logged (Telegram refused the backup message, with Telegram's description) and nothing is posted to the main thread instead.
  • A 429 is retried once after Telegram's retry_after, if that is 30 seconds or less.
  • Neither the token nor the text is ever logged. A connection error is logged by its class only — the URL, and so the token, is in the message of several of them.
  • The HTTP client logs every request with its URL at INFO, and the Bot API's URL holds the token: a filter on the httpx2 logger writes <redacted> in its place (and in place of a webhook's URL), however the project configured its logging.

docs.title: Through django-aiogram
docs.text:
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[aiogram]' — the project's own bot, configured where django-aiogram is; no token here.

'NOTIFY': [
    {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.django_aiogram.TopicNotifier',
        'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
        'TOPIC_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID', ''),
        # 'DELIVERY': 'queue',   # through the bot container; 'direct' by default
        # 'BOT': 'ops',          # one of TELEGRAM_BOTS; the default bot when absent
    },
],

CHAT_ID is required (0 counts as unset); TOPIC_ID is validated by the same check as for Telegram above (E010).

docs.title: Direct or queued
docs.text:
DELIVERY decides which of the bot's methods carries the message:

'direct' (default) 'queue' calls bot.send_raw('send_message', ...) bot.send('send_message', ...) who talks to Telegram the process running the pass — the worker, the deploy's one-off container the bot container, which consumes django-aiogram's queue the bot token must be in the worker's (and the deploy container's) environment stays in the bot container; the worker needs only the queue True from the notifier means sent — synchronously where no bot loop runs; in a process whose bot loop runs, send_raw only schedules the call, and it means "handed over" queued: delivery depends on the bot container running a refusal (wrong topic, bot not in the chat) logged here — whether it raises follows django-aiogram's RAISE_EXCEPTION; either way the backup goes on logged by the bot container, not here django-aiogram's queue: rate limiting, event log, correlation ids bypassed, with the queue applied

Choose direct when the process running the pass may hold the token, and the message should not depend on another container. Choose queue when the project runs a dedicated bot container and keeps the token there: one place talks to Telegram, under one rate limit — and while that container is down, backup messages are not delivered.

docs.title: Another bot wrapper: BOT_FACTORY
docs.text:
'BOT_FACTORY': 'acme.bots.backup_bot',

A dotted path to a callable that takes no arguments and returns an object with send_raw(method, **kwargs) and/or send(method, **kwargs) — whichever DELIVERY calls. It replaces BOT: the escape hatch for an older django-aiogram, or any other wrapper that can be adapted to those two methods. It is called at every send; a path that does not import, or does not name a callable, is E002.

docs.title: A webhook
docs.text:
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[webhook]' — a JSON POST to any URL, with httpx2: an incident tool, a chat that takes webhooks, your own endpoint.

'NOTIFY': [
    {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.webhook.WebhookNotifier',
        'URL': os.environ.get('BACKUP_WEBHOOK_URL', ''),
        'SECRET': os.environ.get('BACKUP_WEBHOOK_SECRET', ''),
        # 'HEADERS': {'Authorization': 'Bearer ...'},
        # 'TIMEOUT': 10, 'RETRIES': 2,
    },
],
option URL required; http:// or https://, else E010 SECRET optional; signs every body (below) HEADERS a mapping of extra headers, e.g. an Authorization; not a mapping is E010 TIMEOUT seconds per attempt, default 10; not a positive number is E010 RETRIES attempts after the first on a network error, a 429 or a 5xx, default 2, waiting 1 s, 2 s, 4 s…; not a whole number ≥ 0 is E010

The body is the outcome as data beside the formatted text, so a receiver can route on kind and still show the message:

{
  "kind": "written",
  "prefix": "acme/prod",
  "env": "prod",
  "name": "",
  "reason": "nightly",
  "error": "",
  "summary": {"stamp": "2026-03-10T03-00Z", "bytes": 5570142208, "keys": ["acme/prod/db/2026-03-10T03-00Z.sql.zst.age", "..."], "seconds": 1044.2, "failed": {}, "removed": [], "depth": {"nights": 14, "since": "2026-02-25"}, "...": "..."},
  "drill": null,
  "newest": null,
  "text": "💾 <b>Backup written</b>: ...",
  "sent_at": "2026-03-10T03:17:24.981Z"
}

kind is written, failed, missing, unchecked, drilled or drill_failed; times are ISO 8601. With a SECRET, every request carries

X-Offsite-Backup-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of the exact body bytes, keyed with SECRET>

— recompute it over the raw body and compare in constant time before trusting the body:

import hashlib, hmac
