expected = 'sha256=' + hmac.new(secret.encode(), request.body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, request.headers['X-Offsite-Backup-Signature']):
    return 403

sent_at is inside the signed body, so a receiver can also refuse a replay of an old one. Any other answer than a 2xx, 429 or 5xx is final. The URL is never logged — a webhook URL often carries its own token — nor the body or the secret: a failure is logged as Webhook refused or unreachable with the status or the error's class.

docs.title: The log
docs.text:
'NOTIFY': [{'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.log.LogNotifier'}],

Writes to the offsite_backup logger: INFO for a written backup and a passed drill, ERROR for anything else, the text in the record's ob_text extra field. It reaches no network, so it keeps working under tests.

docs.title: A notifier never costs the backup
docs.text: Every send is wrapped: a notifier that raises, times out or is misconfigured is logged (Notifier raised, Notifier not built) and the pass goes on. A notifier outage never turns a written backup into a failed one, and never hides a real failure behind its own. The exit status of the command is the pass's, not the chat's.

docs.title: Tests never notify
docs.text: The package's pytest plugin and OffsiteBackupTestRunner silence every notifier that can reach the network for the whole test run, whatever the environment holds. See Testing.

docs.title: Your own notifier
docs.text:
from offsite_backup.notifiers.base import Notifier


class SlackNotifier(Notifier):
    REQUIRED = ('WEBHOOK_URL',)

    def send(self, outcome, text):
        try:
            ...  # post text; outcome.kind is 'written', 'failed', 'missing', 'unchecked', 'drilled' or 'drill_failed'
        except Exception:
            return False
        return True

send() must not raise and answers whether the message was delivered. Leave REACHES_NETWORK = True (the default) for anything that leaves the process, so tests silence it.

docs.title: Your own format
docs.text:
MESSAGES is a dotted path to a callable taking an Outcome and returning the text, or to a module holding one called format_outcome:

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {..., 'MESSAGES': 'acme.backups.format_outcome'}

offsite_backup.outcome.Outcome carries kind, prefix, env, name, reason, summary (objects uploaded, bytes, seconds, removed, failed databases, depth), error, for the morning check newest, stale_hours and now, and for a drill drill (the stamp, the target, a record per database and per archive, what failed, seconds). Outcome.as_dict() is all of it as JSON-ready data — what the webhook sends. A formatter that raises is logged (Backup message not formatted) and nothing is sent — the outcome itself still stands. offsite_backup.messages.default is the reference; its reason_line() and reason_tag() are reusable.

docs.title: Without Django
docs.text:
The passes do not need a Django project. A server that runs a database and a service — a self-hosted application, an identity provider, a registry — gets the same backups from the offsite-backup command: the same stores and Object Lock read back, the same age encryption, the same sources, whole-night rotation, morning check, drill and messages. The setting is a TOML file whose top level is what OFFSITE_BACKUP holds in a Django project.

It is also what replaces a server's own copy of a backup script: the script keeps deciding what leaves (it knows the service), and hands the files to offsite-backup, which decides how — and stops drifting from every other copy.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The command needs Python 3.10+ and no Django. Install it as a tool, with the extras the setting names:

pipx install 'django-offsite-backup[cli,s3,telegram]'
# or: uv tool install 'django-offsite-backup[cli,s3,telegram]'
offsite-backup --version

[cli] adds tomli on Python 3.10 only (3.11+ read TOML with the standard library). The server needs the same binaries as any pass: zstd, age, and pg_dump / psql / pg_restore of at least the database server's major for a PostgreSQL source (Installation). python -m offsite_backup is the same command.

docs.title: The setting
docs.text:
# /etc/offsite-backup/registry.toml — root, 0600
PREFIX = "acme/registry"
ENV = "prod"
NAME = "the registry"

[STORE]
BACKEND = "offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store"
ENDPOINT_URL = "https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com"
REGION = "fsn1"
BUCKET = "acme-backups"
ACCESS_KEY = "${BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY}"
SECRET_KEY = "${BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY}"
LOCK_DAYS = 13

[ENCRYPTION]
BACKEND = "offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli"
RECIPIENTS = "age1..."

[DATABASES]
BACKEND = "offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource"
FORMAT = "custom"
ALIASES = ["default"]

[DATABASES.CONNECTIONS.default]
HOST = "127.0.0.1"
PORT = "5432"
USER = "registry"
PASSWORD = "${REGISTRY_DB_PASSWORD}"
NAME = "registry"

[CONFIG]
BACKEND = "offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource"
PATHS = ["/srv/registry/docker-compose.yml", "/srv/registry/config"]

[RETENTION]
KEEP_NIGHTS = 14

[[NOTIFY]]
BACKEND = "offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier"
TOKEN = "${BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN}"
CHAT_ID = "${BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID}"
TOPIC_ID = "${BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID}"

Every key and option is the one Settings describes, with its default and its check. What differs off Django:

  • Variables. A string may name environment variables: ${NAME}, or ${NAME:-default}; $$ is a literal $. An unset variable is blank — and blank is unset, so a missing secret is still named by E001 instead of read as a value. Only strings expand; write numbers (LOCK_DAYS, KEEP_NIGHTS) as TOML numbers.
  • --env-file FILE (repeatable) reads KEY=value lines — # comments, an optional export, one pair of quotes dropped — for the variables. Later files win over earlier ones and over the process environment. Keep the secrets there, root-only, and the TOML file free of them: neither ever reaches argv.
  • Databases are named in CONNECTIONS, an alias each, with the keys Django's DATABASES has (HOST, PORT, USER, PASSWORD, NAME, OPTIONS). ALIASES says which are dumped — ['default'] unless set (Databases). MySQLSource and SQLiteSource take CONNECTIONS the same way (for SQLite, NAME is the file).
  • Every backend runs here but one. The stores (one or several), both sealers (age and Pyrage), every database source, and the media sources DirectorySource, S3Source and VolumeSource (a Docker volume, through the docker CLI) need no Django. StorageSource reads a Django storage and is refused by name: E002, with [django] as the extra to install where Django is absent, or "needs a Django project" where it is installed and there is no project.
  • Paths are best written absolute; a relative one is the working directory's, as under Django. RENDER_ENV is the exception: it is read against the setting file's directory, where Django would read BASE_DIR. A media DirectorySource needs its ROOT — there is no MEDIA_ROOT to default to.
  • No guard. The once-per-night guard is a Django cache or a database lock; cron fires once, so it is not needed. Wrap the line in flock -n if a slow pass could meet the next.
  • The checks are offsite-backup checks rather than manage.py check — the same codes, without the ones about Django's cache (W003) and test runner (W004).

--config FILE names the setting, or OFFSITE_BACKUP_CONFIG in the environment.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
command what exit run [--without-media] [--reason R] [--only KIND] [--path P] a pass now; --path adds a file or directory to the configuration archive (repeatable) — or, with no [CONFIG], makes one of them alone 0, 1 on failure check the morning check — MISSING / UNCHECKED said through the notifiers 0, 1 status [--json] [--prometheus FILE] [--stale-hours H] the newest whole backup's age per kind, said to nobody (Monitoring) 0 fresh, 1 stale, 2 store unreadable list [--kind K] [--store NAME] [--json] what the store holds per kind 0, 1 restore --stamp S [--identity F] [--into DIR] [--kind K] [--database ALIAS] [--path P] [--store NAME] download, decrypt, verify — one database (--database narrows --kind), or some media files (--path, repeatable, checked against the manifests); --apply --database ALIAS [--from-database A] [--clean] loads a CONNECTIONS alias (Restore) 0, 1 drill [--identity F] [--database ALIAS] [--without-media] the restore drill (Restore) 0, 1 checks [--deploy] the system checks, printed; --deploy adds the bucket's lock, pg_dump against the server, the paths and the drill's target 0, 1 on an error, 3 when backups are off failed [--reason R] TEXT say that something before the pass failed — a dump that died in the caller's script — as the same FAILED message 0

Every command but checks, restore and drill says "not configured on this machine, nothing to do" and exits 0 where backups are off; a usage error (no setting, a file that is not there, TOML that does not parse) is 2. A failure is printed on stderr in one line; the offsite_backup logger writes to stderr as well (Monitoring).

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
CRON_TZ=UTC
0 3 * * *  root  flock -n /run/offsite-backup.lock offsite-backup --config /etc/offsite-backup/registry.toml --env-file /etc/offsite-backup/registry.env run --reason nightly
0 9 * * *  root  offsite-backup --config /etc/offsite-backup/registry.toml --env-file /etc/offsite-backup/registry.env check

Or set OFFSITE_BACKUP_CONFIG in the crontab and drop --config. A systemd timer works the same way; the exit status is what OnFailure= sees.

docs.title: A service that makes its own backup
docs.text:
Some services have their own backup tool, which writes an archive the database dump alone does not replace. Keep the script that knows the service; let it hand the result over:

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
reason=${1:-nightly}
backup() { offsite-backup --config /etc/offsite-backup/app.toml --env-file /etc/offsite-backup/app.env "$@"; }

# off is not a failure; configured by halves is
state=0; backup checks >/dev/null || state=$?
[ "$state" -eq 3 ] && exit 0
[ "$state" -eq 0 ] || exit 1

work=$(mktemp -d /var/backups/app/.work-XXXXXX)
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
app-backup-tool --out "$work/app.tar" \
  || { backup failed --reason "$reason" "the application backup failed; the journal has why"; exit 1; }

backup run --reason "$reason" --path "$work/app.tar" --path /srv/app/app.conf
  • checks answers 3 for "off", 1 for "configured by halves", 0 for "on" — the three states, for a script.
  • failed reports a failure the script met before the pass, in the same message format, so the chat reads the same whichever stage broke.
  • run --reason upgrade, before an upgrade the script performs, says on failure that the upgrade stops and the running service (NAME) keeps serving.
  • --path files go into the configuration archive, <PREFIX>/config/<stamp>.tar.zst.age, last in the pass — so the morning check, status and rotation read it like any other.
  • LAST_SUCCESS_FILE writes the time of every successful pass, for a monitor that reads a file's age.

docs.title: Coming from a hand-written script
docs.text: A script that wrote <PREFIX>/<stamp>.tar.zst.age directly under its prefix leaves those objects where they are: the package writes under <PREFIX>/<kind>/ and rotates only inside each kind's folder, so it never reads or deletes the old layout. Delete the old objects by hand once their locks have run out — or start the package under a new prefix. The message format is the package's; the reasons nightly, deploy, manual and upgrade read as before.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
The same entry point, for a deployment tool written in Python:

from offsite_backup.cli import main

exit_code = main(['--config', '/etc/offsite-backup/app.toml', 'run', '--reason', 'upgrade'])

Or the functions themselves, after offsite_backup.conf.configure(values) with the setting as a dict: offsite_backup.run(), check_last_night(), freshness(), run_drill(). configure(None) goes back to Django's settings; main() does that itself when it returns.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text: A backup nobody has restored is a hope. This page is the procedure, and a drill to run every month so the procedure is known to work before the day it is needed.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The private key — from your password manager. Never copy it to the production server for a routine restore; restore from your own machine, or from a throwaway one.
  • A machine with the project's image (or a checkout with the package installed), age (or the [pyrage] extra — either opens what the other sealed), zstd, and the database's client: psql/pg_restore of the server's major version or newer, mysql / mariadb for MySQL and MariaDB; nothing for SQLite.
  • Settings that point at the same store and PREFIX. A read-only S3 key is enough and better than the server's.

The private key is given as a file (--identity FILE) or in the AGE_IDENTITY environment variable — never as an argument, which ps would show. From the variable it is written to a 0600 file in a private temporary directory for age, and removed with it.

docs.title: 1. See what there is
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_list

acme/prod/
  config/: 14 nights since 2026-02-25, 19 objects, 0.4 MB, newest 2026-03-10T14-12Z, locked until 2026-03-23T14:12:31+00:00, 5 without media
  db/: 14 nights since 2026-02-25, 19 objects, 410.2 MB, newest 2026-03-10T14-12Z, locked until 2026-03-23T14:12:31+00:00, 5 without media
  media/: 14 nights since 2026-02-25, 28 objects, 74322.0 MB, newest 2026-03-10T03-00Z, locked until 2026-03-23T03:02:10+00:00

--kind db narrows it (repeat for several); --json is for scripts. With several stores it lists the first; --store NAME lists another.

docs.title: 2. Download and decrypt
docs.text:
export AGE_IDENTITY="$(cat ~/secure/backup-acme-prod.key)"      # or --identity FILE
python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --into ./restore

restore/config/2026-03-10T03-00Z.tar
restore/db/2026-03-10T03-00Z.sql  (verified)
restore/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.tar
restore/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.002.tar
  • --stamp latest is the newest whole backup (the newest night in config/, or in db/ without a configuration archive); a pass without media is not "whole". Give a stamp such as --stamp 2026-03-10T14-12Z to take any pass, a deploy's included.
  • Every object of that stamp is downloaded, decrypted and — if it starts with zstd's magic bytes — decompressed, into <into>/<kind>/. --into defaults to ./restore-<stamp>.
  • --kind db (repeatable) takes only some kinds — skip a night's media when you need the database. --database ALIAS takes that one database's dump (its kind, db or db-<alias>) and nothing else; beside --kind it narrows — a --kind list without that database is refused rather than widened.
  • --store NAME reads from another of several stores — the local copy while the off-site one is out of reach, or the other way round. The first store is the default, for every command and function on this page (store= in Python).
  • Every database dump is verified: a plain dump must end with PostgreSQL database dump complete; a custom-format one must pass pg_restore --list. A dump that fails says so and stops.
  • Backups copied under <PREFIX>/released/ are not part of a stamp; restore those with --apply and the full key (below).

What you get:

kind file open with db, db-<alias> <stamp>.sql (plain) or <stamp>.dump (custom) psql, pg_restore media, media-<name> <stamp>.<NNN>.tar, one per volume, and <stamp>.<NNN>.manifest.json beside each tar -xf — each volume on its own; the manifest lists its files config <stamp>.tar tar -xf; rendered.env is the environment

A custom-format dump under a legacy .sql… name — written by a predecessor that named its custom dumps .sql.zst.age — just works: the format is read from the magic bytes (PGDMP), not from the name. It is verified with pg_restore --list and loaded with pg_restore by --apply. The file --into writes keeps the object's name (<stamp>.sql), so open it with pg_restore, not psql; head -c 5 on it prints PGDMP for a custom dump.

docs.title: 3. Load a database
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --apply --database default
  • --apply --database ALIAS downloads, decrypts, verifies and loads the dump into that DATABASES alias — with psql --single-transaction for plain SQL, pg_restore --single-transaction --exit-on-error for the custom format, both --no-owner.
  • With --apply, --stamp latest means the newest dump of that database, a deploy's included — the most recent state is what you want back.
  • --stamp also takes a full key: --stamp acme/prod/released/db-tenant_42/2026-03-01T10-00Z.sql.zst.age.

  • --from-database ALIAS loads another alias's backup — production's default into a scratch database:

    python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --apply --database scratch --from-database default

  • The target must be empty. --clean replaces a non-empty one: for PostgreSQL it runs DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public; first (objects in other schemas are not dropped); for MySQL and MariaDB it drops every table and view; for SQLite the file is overwritten. MySQL dumps load through mysql / mariadb, SQLite through the online backup API (Databases).

From Python:

from offsite_backup import restore_database

restore_database('latest', 'scratch', identity='~/secure/backup-acme-prod.key', source_alias='default')
restore_database('2026-03-10T03-00Z', 'default', clean=True)  # identity from AGE_IDENTITY

restore_database(source, alias, *, identity=None, clean=False, source_alias=None, identity_text=None, store=None) answers with the key it loaded.

identity_text is the private key's text, for code that holds it rather than a file: it is written to a private 0600 temporary file for age and removed afterwards. It is meant for a dedicated, narrowly used identity the server holds on purpose — the wake key of a one-off backup — never the backups' main key, which stays off the server. Passing both identity and identity_text is refused (MisconfiguredError).

restore_database(key, 'tenant_42', identity_text=settings.WAKE_IDENTITY)

docs.title: Some media files
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --path invoices/2026/03 --path logo.png --into ./restore

restore/media/invoices/2026/03/0001.pdf  (verified)
restore/media/invoices/2026/03/0002.pdf  (verified)
restore/media/logo.png  (verified)

--path (repeatable) is a file's name in the archive, or a folder: everything under it (invoices/2026 takes invoices/2026/..., never invoices/2026-old/...). Every volume has a manifest; the restore downloads the manifests, then only the volumes that hold a match, extracts the matches under <into>/<kind>/, and checks each file against the SHA-256 its manifest recorded — (verified). A file that differs, or a manifest promising a file its volume lacks, stops the restore with an error. A volume written before manifests existed (0.3 and earlier) is downloaded and searched whole, and its files are not verified. --kind media-private narrows it to one source; --path does not combine with --database or --apply.

from offsite_backup.restore import restore_media

restored = restore_media('latest', ['invoices/2026/03'], into=Path('restore'), identity='key.txt')

docs.title: Everything
docs.text:
mkdir -p media && for v in restore/media/*.tar; do tar -xf "$v" -C media; done
mkdir -p deploy && tar -xf restore/config/*.tar -C deploy

Names in a media volume are relative to the source's ROOT (or are the full object keys, for an S3 source). Copy them back into the volume, directory or bucket the application reads. rendered.env is the environment the release ran with — the file to rebuild .env from on a new machine.

docs.title: Rebuilding a lost machine
docs.text:
1. Provision the machine; install Docker.
  2. backup_restore --stamp latest --into ./restore on your own machine.
  3. Unpack the configuration archive and copy its deployment directory to the new machine; rebuild .env from rendered.env (and rotate any secret you suspect left with the old machine).
  4. Start the database; backup_restore --stamp latest --apply --database default from inside the new deployment, with AGE_IDENTITY set for that one command only — or load the dump you already decrypted in step 2 with psql/pg_restore, and the private key never touches the server.
  5. Unpack the media volumes into the media volume or bucket.
  6. Start the application; run backup_offsite --reason manual and check the message.

docs.title: The monthly drill
docs.text:
Restoring is a skill that decays, and a backup that was never restored is a hope. The drill does what a person would, end to end, and says the outcome where the backups are said:

python manage.py backup_drill                     # or: offsite-backup drill
python manage.py backup_drill --without-media     # the volumes are the slow part
  1. The newest whole pass is found (as --stamp latest) and every object of it downloaded and decrypted — the identity from --identity FILE, DRILL['IDENTITY_FILE'] or AGE_IDENTITY.
  2. Every database dump is verified, then restored into DRILL['DATABASE'], a throwaway database the project names — emptied first (PostgreSQL: every schema but the system ones dropped; MySQL and MariaDB: every table and view; SQLite: every table, view and trigger of the file), loaded, and every table counted there with count(*). For SQLite the target is a file, and a target naming the live file by another path is refused like a live alias.
  3. With DRILL['COMPARE_LIVE'] (on by default), the live database is counted too, and the message shows both. Rows are compared, not required to match: production kept writing after the backup. A table the live database has and the restore lacks is named (⚠️ Not in the backup, live now: ...) — a migration since the pass, or a hole — without failing the drill. A live database that cannot be counted is logged and left uncompared.
  4. Every media volume and the configuration archive is decrypted and read to its end as a tar (unless DRILL['MEDIA'] is false or --without-media is given) — files and bytes counted. A volume's manifest is not opened: it describes the volume, which is.
  5. The throwaway database is emptied again and the workspace removed, whatever happened.
  6. The outcome goes through the notifiers: Restore drill passed with a line per database and per kind of archive, or Restore drill FAILED naming every object that did not come back and the step it failed at (Notifications). One database that does not restore does not stop the others; the command exits non-zero at the end, naming each.
OFFSITE_BACKUP = {
    ...,
    'DRILL': {
        'DATABASE': 'drill',                          # an alias in DATABASES (or CONNECTIONS off Django)
        'IDENTITY_FILE': '/run/secrets/drill.key',    # or AGE_IDENTITY, or --identity
        # 'MEDIA': False,                             # leave the volumes unopened
        # 'COMPARE_LIVE': False,                      # never count the live database
    },
}
DATABASES['drill'] = {**DATABASES['default'], 'HOST': 'scratch-db', 'NAME': 'drill'}

Never the live database. The drill refuses a target that is a database it backs up — the same alias, or another alias with the same host (localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1 are one), port (an empty one is 5432) and name — before it reads the store, and again for every database the pass wrote. check --deploy reports that, or a target that names no database at all, as E011, before the month it would run. What the drill does to its target is destructive by design: point it at a database that holds nothing you want.

From Python, offsite_backup.run_drill(identity=None, identity_text=None, database=None, media=None) returns the report (stamp, target, databases, archives, seconds) and raises DrillFailedError naming what failed.

docs.title: Where it runs: the identity
docs.text:
The drill needs the private key, which by design is not on the production server (Security model). Two ways to run it, in order of preference:

  • On a machine of its own — a small drill host or a CI job with the identity, a read-only store key and a scratch PostgreSQL. It needs no copy of the project: the command line runs the drill from a TOML setting with the same PREFIX, STORE and ENCRYPTION, a DATABASES block whose CONNECTIONS hold the drill's alias, and COMPARE_LIVE off (the live database is out of reach there).
  • In the project's scheduler — beat_schedule(drill=...) or register(broker, drill=...) (Scheduling). Simple, and it compares with the live database — but the worker then holds a key that opens every backup sealed to it. Accept that only knowingly; seal the backups to a second recipient whose key exists only for the drill, so it can be rotated on its own.

docs.title: A database source of your own
docs.text: The drill asks the database source two more things than a pass does: tables(alias), every table with its row count, and clear(alias), empty the throwaway database — PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite answer both; same_database() decides what counts as the live one (host, port and name; for SQLite, the file). A source that does not implement them fails the drill by its name, and the rest still runs.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
The steps the command automates, for a machine that cannot run it:

  1. backup_restore --stamp latest --into ./drill; note the stamp and that every dump says (verified).
  2. Start a clean PostgreSQL of the same major as production (docker run -d --name drill -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=drill -p 55432:5432 postgres:18).
  3. Load the dump into it — psql/pg_restore, or backup_restore --stamp <stamp> --apply --database drill --from-database default.

  4. Count every table in both databases and compare:

    SELECT format('SELECT %L AS t, count(*) FROM %I.%I', table_name, table_schema, table_name)
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_type = 'BASE TABLE'
ORDER BY table_name \gexec

  5. Unpack one media volume and open a few files; unpack the configuration archive and read rendered.env — is every variable the application needs there?

  6. Write down the date, the stamp, the table count and how long it took. Delete the drill database and ./drill.

docs.title: Retention and locks
docs.text:
'RETENTION': {'KEEP_NIGHTS': 14},
'STORE': {..., 'LOCK_DAYS': 13},

Each kind keeps its newest 14 whole nights; every object is locked for 13 days. One less, on purpose.

docs.title: Counted in whole nights
docs.text:
Retention counts calendar nights in UTC, read from the object's name — not objects, and not age:

  • not objects, because a night's media is several volumes, and a night with ten volumes would otherwise push out nine nights of databases;
  • not stamps, because a project runs several passes a day — the nightly one, one per deploy, one by hand — and counting each would push out nights whose lock still holds;
  • not the store's timestamps, because the name is what a person reads in a listing and what every store keeps the same way.

2026-03-10T03-00Z and 2026-03-10T14-12Z are one night: 2026-03-10. A key whose name carries no stamp is not a backup and is never touched.

Each kind folder rotates on its own — db/, db-analytics/, media/, config/ — and strictly inside <PREFIX>/<kind>/, with the trailing slash: db/ never matches db-analytics/, and acme/prod/ never matches acme/prod-old/. A pass rotates the kinds it wrote to, so a nightly pass rotates media and a deploy pass does not.

docs.title: Rotation runs last
docs.text: Only after every part of the pass is uploaded. Making room before the new backup exists is how a bad night becomes an empty bucket. A pass that failed before the end — an upload, a lock read-back, a media volume — rotates nothing. A pass in which only a database dump failed does rotate; the failed database's folder simply has no new night, so it keeps its newest 14 as before.

docs.title: Passes without media
docs.text:
A deploy pass writes the databases and the configuration and leaves the media to the night. Its objects are marked .without-media.:

acme/prod/db/2026-03-10T14-12Z.without-media.sql.zst.age

Those objects never count as nights. They are kept while they are newer than the oldest whole night kept, and deleted with it. Counted naively, a fortnight of deploys over failing nights would push out the last whole backup's database while its media stayed — unrestorable.

With no whole night at all — a fresh setup that has seen only deploys — partial nights are counted by themselves, so the folder cannot grow without bound.

The marker is written only in a project that has MEDIA configured. Where there is no media, a pass without media is a whole backup, and counts as one.

docs.title: Versions and delete markers
docs.text: On a versioned bucket, deleting a key without a version id only writes a delete marker: the bytes stay stored and billed. Rotation therefore lists every version of every key in the folder — markers included — and deletes each by version id. An expired key leaves nothing behind.

docs.title: Locks: why one day less
docs.text:
A COMPLIANCE lock cannot be shortened or removed by anyone until it runs out — that is its point. Rotation deletes the 15th-newest night; with 13-day locks, everything it reaches is unlocked already. E007 refuses KEEP_NIGHTS <= LOCK_DAYS:

?: (offsite_backup.E007) RETENTION['KEEP_NIGHTS'] is 13, not more than OFFSITE_BACKUP['STORE']['LOCK_DAYS'] = 13.
    HINT: Keep at least one night more than the lock (e.g. 14 nights, 13 days), so rotation only ever deletes objects whose lock has run out.

A version that is still locked when rotation reaches it — a night of several passes, a clock that disagrees — is left for a later night with a warning in the log (Backup still locked; left for a later night), not a failure: a refused delete must not fail the night over an object that is safe.

Changing either number:

  • more nights — raise KEEP_NIGHTS and leave LOCK_DAYS;
  • longer locks — raise LOCK_DAYS, change the bucket's default rule to the same number (E006), and keep KEEP_NIGHTS above it (E007). Objects already written keep the lock they were given.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text:
After rotation the pass reads how far back the backups reach — the number of distinct nights under the first database's folder (the configuration's, without databases) whose current version is an object, and the oldest of them:

🗄 Kept: 14 days, since 2026-02-25

The count includes nights that only a deploy pass wrote. It is best effort: a depth that cannot be read is a line left out of the message, never a failed backup.

docs.title: Storage, roughly
docs.text: A kind holds about KEEP_NIGHTS nights of whole backups plus every deploy pass since the oldest of them. Media is uploaded whole every night, so it dominates: 5 GB of media at 14 nights is about 70 GB stored. Incremental media is on the roadmap, for when that stops being acceptable.

docs.title: S3 providers
docs.text:
Whatever the provider, the bucket needs three things, and the first one is only possible at creation:

  1. Object Lock, enabled when the bucket is created (versioning comes with it);
  2. a default retention rule of COMPLIANCE, LOCK_DAYS days — 13 unless you changed it;
  3. a key for the backup alone.

Then python manage.py check --deploy on the server: no E005, no E006, and the bucket is ready. Run a first pass with media (volumes go up multipart, which is what the default rule is for) and look for Backup written before trusting it.

The examples use the AWS CLI, which talks to every provider below with --endpoint-url.

docs.title: Addressing style
docs.text:
An S3 client names the bucket either in the path (https://host/bucket/key) or in the host name (https://bucket.host/key, virtual-hosted). ADDRESSING_STYLE on the store and on an S3Source sets it — 'auto' (default, botocore decides), 'path' or 'virtual':

provider ADDRESSING_STYLE Hetzner Object Storage either works AWS S3 'virtual', or leave it 'auto' MinIO 'path' SeaweedFS 'path'

SIGNATURE_VERSION (botocore's, e.g. 's3v4') and VERIFY (False, or the path of a CA bundle for a server behind an internal certificate) sit in the same block — Settings.

docs.title: Hetzner Object Storage
docs.text:
The provider this package's S3 rules were measured on.

One Hetzner project per product or client. Hetzner's S3 credentials belong to a project and reach every bucket in it; they cannot be narrowed to a bucket or a prefix. A key leaked from one product's server must not open another's backups, so each product — and each client — gets its own project, its own bucket and its own key. Services of your own that share a trust boundary may share one bucket, a PREFIX each.

  1. Create the project, then the S3 credentials in it (Security → S3 credentials). The secret is shown once.

  2. Create the bucket with Object Lock. It cannot be enabled later; a bucket created without it has to be replaced. With the AWS CLI:

    export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
ENDPOINT=https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com     # nbg1, hel1, ... — the bucket's location

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket acme-backups \
    --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT"

    If you create it in the console instead, tick Object Lock in the creation dialog.

  3. Set the default rule — COMPLIANCE, days equal to LOCK_DAYS:

    aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-backups --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT" \
    --object-lock-configuration \
    '{"ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled", "Rule": {"DefaultRetention": {"Mode": "COMPLIANCE", "Days": 13}}}'

aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-backups --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT"
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket acme-backups --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT"   # "Enabled"

  4. The settings:

    'STORE': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
    'ENDPOINT_URL': 'https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com',
    'REGION': 'fsn1',
    'BUCKET': 'acme-backups',
    'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
    'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
    'LOCK_DAYS': 13,
},

What was measured there, and what the package does about each — the reasoning is on Stores: S3:

  • a single PUT ignored the default rule and landed GOVERNANCE → the lock is an argument of every upload;
  • a multipart upload took its date from the default rule → the rule must equal LOCK_DAYS (E006), and every lock is read back;
  • a single PUT above 5 GB was refused → multipart in 64 MiB parts, volumes of 4 GiB;
  • there is no IAM to withhold "bypass governance" → COMPLIANCE only;
  • a delete without a version id only adds a marker → rotation deletes versions.

docs.title: AWS S3
docs.text:
Leave ENDPOINT_URL empty and set REGION.

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket acme-backups --region eu-central-1 \
    --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=eu-central-1 \
    --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket

aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-backups \
    --object-lock-configuration \
    '{"ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled", "Rule": {"DefaultRetention": {"Mode": "COMPLIANCE", "Days": 13}}}'

AWS can narrow a key to a prefix, so several projects may share a bucket safely. A starting point for the backup user's policy — what a pass, the morning check, backup_list, keep_apart and a restore call, and nothing that changes the bucket:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetBucketVersioning", "s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-backups"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:ListBucketVersions"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-backups",
      "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["acme/prod/*"]}}
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:PutObject", "s3:PutObjectRetention", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload",
        "s3:GetObject", "s3:GetObjectVersion", "s3:GetObjectRetention",
        "s3:DeleteObjectVersion"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-backups/acme/prod/*"
    }
  ]
}

Do not grant s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, s3:PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration, s3:PutBucketVersioning or s3:DeleteBucket. A restore needs only the read actions, and is better done with a separate read-only key from your own machine.

docs.title: MinIO
docs.text:
The package's integration tests run against MinIO with Object Lock and versioning.

mc alias set backups https://minio.example.com "$ACCESS_KEY" "$SECRET_KEY"
mc mb --with-lock backups/acme-backups
mc retention set --default COMPLIANCE 13d backups/acme-backups
mc retention info --default backups/acme-backups

'STORE': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
    'ENDPOINT_URL': 'https://minio.example.com',
    'REGION': 'us-east-1',
    'BUCKET': 'acme-backups',
    'ADDRESSING_STYLE': 'path',
    ...
},

MinIO needs path-style addressing (above).

A MinIO on the same machine as the application is not off-site. Run it elsewhere, or treat it like a directory store.

docs.title: SeaweedFS
docs.text:
SeaweedFS's S3 gateway needs path-style addressing:

'STORE': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
    'ENDPOINT_URL': 'https://s3.example.com',
    'BUCKET': 'acme-backups',
    'ADDRESSING_STYLE': 'path',
    ...
},

The same goes for an S3Source reading media from a SeaweedFS bucket. Whether a given SeaweedFS version supports what the store needs — Object Lock, a default retention rule — is for check --deploy to tell you (E005, E006), as for any provider below.

docs.title: Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 and others
docs.text:
Not yet verified. This package needs, from the S3 API:

  • PutObject and multipart uploads that accept ObjectLockMode and ObjectLockRetainUntilDate, and HeadObject that returns them;
  • GetObjectLockConfiguration with a default retention rule, and GetBucketVersioning;
  • ListObjectVersions with delete markers, and DeleteObject with a VersionId.

Check your provider's S3-compatibility documentation for each of these before relying on it. Then prove it on a throwaway bucket: manage.py check --deploy tells you what the bucket answers (E005, E006), and a pass with a media volume above 64 MiB tells you whether a multipart object lands with the date asked (BackupUnlockedError if not).

A provider that cannot lock objects can still hold backups with LOCK_DAYS: 0 — encrypted, off the machine, and deletable by the key on the server. Say so in your own runbook; the Security model explains what that gives up.

Reports of what works on other providers are welcome as issues.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Two jobs, both in UTC — and a third, monthly, when you ask for it:

job when what the nightly pass 03:00 UTC everything, media included; guarded to once per night the morning check 09:00 UTC is there a whole backup younger than STALE_HOURS? — Monitoring the restore drill off unless scheduled; e.g. the 1st, 05:00 UTC restore the newest whole backup into a throwaway database and report — Restore

Object names, nights and the guard are all UTC, whatever TIME_ZONE says. Run the morning check a few hours after the pass, so a slow night is not reported missing, and early enough in your working day that someone reads it.

docs.title: Celery
docs.text:
# settings.py
from offsite_backup.schedule.celery import beat_schedule

CELERY_TIMEZONE = 'UTC'
CELERY_IMPORTS = ['offsite_backup.schedule.celery']
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {
    **beat_schedule(),                 # nightly 03:00, check 09:00
    # **beat_schedule(nightly=(2, 30), check=(8, 0)),
    ...
}

offsite_backup.schedule.celery defines two shared tasks, offsite_backup.nightly (run_nightly()) and offsite_backup.check (check_last_night()), and beat_schedule(nightly=(3, 0), check=(9, 0)) returns beat entries for both as (hour, minute) crontabs in the beat's timezone. CELERY_IMPORTS makes sure the worker registers the tasks; this assumes the usual app.config_from_object('django.conf:settings', namespace='CELERY').

docs.title: The beat's timezone
docs.text:
The entries are in whatever CELERY_TIMEZONE says, not in UTC. A project whose beat runs in local time has two ways to keep the pass at 03:00 UTC:

Run the beat in UTCPass local hours 
CELERY_TIMEZONE = 'UTC'
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {**beat_schedule(), ...}

Simple, and it shifts every other entry of the beat too: a report scheduled for crontab(hour=8) local time now runs at 08:00 UTC. Rewrite the project's own entries in UTC when you switch.

CELERY_TIMEZONE = 'Europe/Berlin'   # UTC+2 in summer
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {
    **beat_schedule(nightly=(5, 0), check=(11, 0)),   # 03:00 and 09:00 UTC in summer
    ...
}

The other entries stay as they are. A timezone with daylight saving moves the pass by an hour twice a year — harmless: the guard and the nights are UTC dates either way, and STALE_HOURS (26) absorbs the hour.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
The nightly task retries on any error: autoretry_for=(Exception,), max_retries=3 (offsite_backup.schedule.celery.NIGHTLY_RETRIES), retry_backoff=60 — a minute, then two, then four. Object storage is reached over the network, and one transient error should not lose the night. To turn the retries off:

CELERY_TASK_ANNOTATIONS = {'offsite_backup.nightly': {'max_retries': 0}}

The module imports Celery, so only a project that runs Celery imports it.

The check task raises when a backup is missing or the store cannot be read, so the task fails wherever your Celery failures are reported, on top of the chat message.

docs.title: taskiq
docs.text:
# acme/broker.py
from taskiq import TaskiqScheduler
from taskiq.schedule_sources import LabelScheduleSource

from offsite_backup.schedule.taskiq import register

broker = ...  # your broker
backup_nightly, backup_check = register(broker)
# register(broker, nightly='30 2 * * *', check='0 8 * * *')

scheduler = TaskiqScheduler(broker, sources=[LabelScheduleSource(broker)])

register(broker, *, nightly='0 3 * * *', check='0 9 * * *', retries=3) defines the same two tasks, named offsite_backup.nightly and offsite_backup.check, with schedule labels for taskiq's LabelScheduleSource (cron, UTC). The pass is a blocking batch job, so each task runs it in a thread. The worker must have Django set up before the tasks run, as for any task that touches the ORM.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
The nightly task carries the labels retry_on_error=True and max_retries=retries (3 by default). Labels only describe the wish: the broker needs taskiq's SimpleRetryMiddleware to act on them.

from taskiq.middlewares import SimpleRetryMiddleware

broker = YourBroker(...).with_middlewares(SimpleRetryMiddleware())
backup_nightly, backup_check = register(broker)
# register(broker, retries=0)   # no retry labels at all

docs.title: cron, systemd timers, Kubernetes CronJobs
docs.text:
Anything that runs a command on a schedule:

CRON_TZ=UTC
0 3 * * *  cd /app && python manage.py backup_offsite --reason nightly
0 9 * * *  cd /app && python manage.py backup_check

The command is not guarded (below) — cron fires once, so it does not need to be — and not retried. Both commands exit non-zero on failure, so cron's mail, a systemd OnFailure= unit or the CronJob's failed status sees it as well as the chat.

On a server with no Django project, the same jobs are offsite-backup run --reason nightly and offsite-backup check — Without Django.

With Docker Compose and a host crontab:

0 3 * * *  cd /srv/acme && docker compose exec -T worker python manage.py backup_offsite --reason nightly

docs.title: The monthly drill
docs.text:
Off by default in both adapters — it needs a throwaway database (DRILL['DATABASE']) and the private key where it runs; read where it runs first.

# Celery: the 1st of the month, 05:00 in the beat's timezone — (day of month, hour, minute)
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {**beat_schedule(drill=(1, 5, 0)), ...}

# taskiq: a cron expression, UTC
backup_nightly, backup_check = register(broker, drill='0 5 1 * *')
# the drill task: broker.find_task('offsite_backup.drill')

The task is offsite_backup.drill (run_drill()). It is not retried: a drill that failed has said why, and another attempt would restore the same backup again. It skips where backups are off, and otherwise raises on failure, so the scheduler's own failure report fires beside the chat's. Without a scheduler:

0 5 1 * *  cd /app && python manage.py backup_drill

docs.title: Retries and the guard
docs.text:
Both adapters retry the nightly task only. A failed pass gives the night back to the guard (below), so a retry re-enters through it and runs the pass again; a pass that succeeds marks the night done once. Each attempt that fails sends its own FAILED message, so a transient error the retries absorbed shows as one or more FAILED messages followed by a written one.

The morning check is not retried: each attempt would only say MISSING again.

docs.title: Once per night
docs.text: A deploy that recreates the scheduler around the nightly time fired the nightly task twice — the old scheduler as it stopped, the new one as it started. Two passes in one night double the upload and race each other's rotation. So run_nightly() — what both adapters call — claims the UTC night where every worker sees it. GUARD['BACKEND'] says where: a shared Django cache ('cache', the default) or a PostgreSQL advisory lock ('database').

docs.title: The cache backend
docs.text:
1. a night already done is skipped;
  2. otherwise it claims running with an atomic cache.add (held for RUNNING_SECONDS, an hour); a night someone else is running is skipped;
  3. it looks for done again under the claim, in case it finished in between;
  4. on failure it releases the claim and re-raises, so the scheduler's retry can run tonight;
  5. on success it writes done (kept DONE_SECONDS, 26 hours — past the end of its UTC date) before releasing running, so there is no moment when neither is set.

A pass whose worker died holds the night for an hour at most. The keys are offsite_backup:<PREFIX>:<YYYY-MM-DD>:done and :running.

'GUARD': {'CACHE': 'default'},   # ENABLED True, RUNNING_SECONDS 3600, DONE_SECONDS 93600

The cache must be shared between the workers and the schedulers: Redis, Memcached, the database cache. A LocMemCache or DummyCache is per process and guards nothing; W003 says so. A CACHE alias missing from CACHES is E001. 'GUARD': {'ENABLED': False} turns the claim off.

docs.title: The database backend
docs.text:
'GUARD': {'BACKEND': 'database'},   # DATABASE 'default'

For a project with no shared cache — one that would otherwise configure Redis for the guard alone. The databases this package dumps are PostgreSQL, so a project that has them already has what the lock needs: no new dependency, and a database every worker reaches is shared by construction.

  1. running is a PostgreSQL session advisory lock (pg_try_advisory_lock) on GUARD['DATABASE'] (default 'default'), with a key derived from PREFIX — so two projects sharing one database server do not block each other. A night someone else is running is skipped.
  2. done is asked of the store itself: under the lock, a whole backup stamped with tonight's UTC date in config/ and in every database's folder means the night is done, and it is skipped. No cache at all. (With neither config nor databases, the media folders answer.)
  3. On failure or success the lock is released. A pass where one database failed still uploads the others and the config — but that database's folder has nothing for tonight, so the retry runs the pass again.

There is no RUNNING_SECONDS: a worker that dies mid-pass closes its connection, and the server releases the lock at that moment. GUARD['DATABASE'] must be a PostgreSQL alias of DATABASES (E001 otherwise, and for an unknown BACKEND); W003 does not apply. CACHE, RUNNING_SECONDS and DONE_SECONDS are not read.

Passes by hand and deploy passes are never guarded: they are meant to run whenever someone asks.

docs.title: Calling it yourself
docs.text:
from offsite_backup import run, run_nightly, check_last_night

run_nightly()  # guarded; None when skipped or when backups are off
run(reason='manual')  # one pass now; Summary, or raises
run(media=False, reason='deploy')
run(only=['db'])  # 'db', 'media', 'config'
check_last_night()  # oldest of the newest whole backups; raises when missing

run() raises NotConfiguredError on a machine where backups are off; the commands and run_nightly() check first and do nothing there.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: The design goal in one line: the machine that writes a backup cannot read one, and cannot destroy one it has written. This page says how far that holds, and where it stops.

docs.title: What sits where
docs.text: where secret? age public key(s) server environment (RECIPIENTS) no age private key your password manager, off the machine yes — opens every backup S3 key for the store server environment yes — writes, lists, reads ciphertext S3 key for an S3 media source server environment yes — reads the media bucket notifier token server environment, or django-aiogram's settings yes database password server environment; PGPASSWORD for pg_dump, a 0600 option file for mysqldump yes the Docker socket (a VolumeSource only) mounted into the worker yes — root on the host a wake key (optional) server yes — opens only the dumps sealed to it

docs.title: What the server can and cannot do
docs.text:
The server — the application, its worker, anyone who has a shell on it — can:

  • write new backups, list the store, download ciphertext;
  • read the media, the databases, the deployment directory and the environment, because it backs them up;
  • stop backing up.

It cannot:

  • read a backup. Everything is sealed with age to public keys; the private key is not on the machine, and E008 refuses one in RECIPIENTS.
  • delete or shorten a COMPLIANCE-locked object before its lock runs out — not with the key it has — and, on providers that implement COMPLIANCE as AWS does, not with the account's root credentials either. That is what COMPLIANCE means, and why it is the only mode this package uses.
  • send backups somewhere else by accident. The S3 client is built from the configured options only; ambient credentials (~/.aws, instance roles, AWS_*) are ignored.

docs.title: A stolen store key (the server is compromised, or a key leaks)
docs.text:
• Cannot read backups: ciphertext only.
  • Cannot delete a locked object within its lock — 13 days by default. Deleting the key name only adds a delete marker; the locked version stays and can be retrieved by version id with the provider's tools.
  • Can add things on top: new versions of a key or delete markers. backup_restore reads the current version, so after a compromise list the versions (aws s3api list-object-versions) and restore from a version written before it. The morning check only sees current versions, so hiding the recent backups behind markers makes it report them missing.
  • Can delete what is no longer locked: everything older than LOCK_DAYS. The window you can count on after a compromise is LOCK_DAYS, not KEEP_NIGHTS. Notice early — that is what the morning check is for — and raise LOCK_DAYS (with the bucket's default rule and KEEP_NIGHTS) if two weeks is too short for you.
  • Can fill the bucket and so the bill. Provider-side quotas and billing alerts are the answer.
  • On a provider where keys reach every bucket of their project, can do all of the above to every bucket in that project. Hence one project per product or client (S3 providers).

docs.title: GOVERNANCE mode
docs.text: Bypassable by any key holding the "bypass governance retention" permission — on some providers, any key at all. It protects against mistakes, not against an attacker with the server's key. This package never uses it, and the read-back fails a pass where an object lands GOVERNANCE.

docs.title: A directory store
docs.text: No immutability. Anyone who can write to the directory can delete every backup in it, and it is on the machine it protects. It protects against a dropped table, not against a lost machine or an intruder (W001).

docs.title: LOCK_DAYS: 0
docs.text: The same as a directory store, off the machine: encrypted, and deletable by the server's key.

docs.title: The private key
docs.text: Whoever has it can read every backup sealed to it — including the configuration archive, which holds every secret the application has (rendered.env). Keep it off servers, keep it where two people can reach it, and restore from your own machine. If it ever reached a server, make a new pair and treat the old backups as exposed.

docs.title: The drill's key
docs.text: The restore drill decrypts, so wherever it runs holds a private key. Run it on a machine of its own, with a read-only store key and a scratch database, and the production server stays unable to read a backup. Scheduled on the production worker instead, the worker can read every backup sealed to that key — a choice to make knowingly, with a recipient that exists only for the drill and can be rotated on its own. The drill refuses a target that is a live database, and empties its target afterwards, so a copy of production does not stay in the scratch database.

docs.title: The wake key
docs.text: A server that holds an extra identity can open the dumps sealed to it — by design, so it can restore them itself — and nothing else. Seal only the dumps that need it.

docs.title: The Docker socket
docs.text: A VolumeSource reads a volume the worker does not mount, through the Docker daemon — so the worker holds the daemon's socket, and whoever controls the worker can start any container on the host: root on the host. The source itself only creates a container (never starts it), mounts the volume read-only with no network, and reads it with docker cp; the risk is the socket, not what the source does with it. Mount the volume read-only into the worker and use DirectorySource where you can; where you cannot, a socket proxy that allows only volume inspect, create, archive (what docker cp uses) and rm narrows it.

docs.title: Several stores
docs.text: A second store is a second copy, not a second lock: a DirectoryStore beside S3 adds a fast restore and an unlocked copy on the machine. The off-site, locked store is what survives an intruder; a pass that could not write to it fails by its name.

docs.title: What leaves the machine besides backups
docs.text:
• Messages carry the prefix, sizes, durations and, on failure, the first 500 characters of the error — escaped. Errors never include the database password: it travels in PGPASSWORD (PostgreSQL) or a 0600 option file (MySQL, MariaDB), never on a command line. A Telegram transport error is logged by its class only, because its text contains the URL and therefore the token.
  • A webhook receives the outcome as data — the prefix, keys, sizes, the error text — and never a credential; with a SECRET the body is signed so the receiver can refuse a forged one. Its URL is never logged.
  • No message, token, password or private key is logged — the HTTP client's own request line included: the notifiers' token and webhook URL are redacted from it.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Notifiers that reach the network are silenced for every pytest run and under OffsiteBackupTestRunner (or OffsiteBackupRunnerMixin in a project's own runner), --parallel and pytest-xdist workers included. Keep production tokens out of CI test jobs anyway (Testing).

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Please report security issues privately through GitHub's security advisories for the repository rather than in a public issue. See SECURITY.md in the repository.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
One dict, OFFSITE_BACKUP, in settings.py — or, on a server with no Django project, the same keys at the top level of a TOML file (Without Django). Every key has a default; the backends each take a block of their own — BACKEND, a dotted path, plus that backend's options.

import os

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {
    'PREFIX': 'acme/prod',
    'ENV': 'prod',
    'NAME': 'acme',
    'STORE': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
        'ENDPOINT_URL': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT', ''),
        'REGION': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_REGION', ''),
        'BUCKET': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_BUCKET', ''),
        'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
        'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
        'LOCK_DAYS': 13,
    },
    'ENCRYPTION': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
        'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
    },
    'DATABASES': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource',
        'ALIASES': ['default'],
        'FORMAT': 'plain',
    },
    'MEDIA': [
        {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource', 'EXCLUDE': ['thumbs/*']},
    ],
    'CONFIG': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource',
        'PATHS': ['/app/deploy'],
        'RENDER_ENV': 'deploy-vars.txt',
    },
    'RETENTION': {'KEEP_NIGHTS': 14},
    'CHECK': {'STALE_HOURS': 26},
    'NOTIFY': [
        {
            'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier',
            'TOKEN': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN', ''),
            'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
            'TOPIC_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID', ''),
        },
    ],
    'GUARD': {'CACHE': 'default'},
}

Credentials come from the environment, in your settings. The package never reads os.environ for its configuration (the exceptions are AGE_IDENTITY, the private key a restore reads — see Restore — and OFFSITE_BACKUP_SILENCE, the test runner's switch — see Testing; off Django, the command line expands ${NAME} in its TOML file — see Without Django). Read each one with a default of '', as above: an unset variable then means "off", not a KeyError at import.

docs.title: Blank means unset
docs.text:
What os.environ.get('X', '') gives on a machine without X is read as not set, wherever it ends up:

  • None, a blank string and 0 (what int(os.environ.get('X') or 0) gives) are unset. A required option holding one of them is named by E001, like an absent one.
  • A list made only of those — [os.environ.get('X', '')] is [''] — is unset too.
  • Inside a list, blank items are dropped: PATHS, INCLUDE/EXCLUDE, a list of ALIASES, RECIPIENTS.
  • A TOPIC_ID that is unset means the chat's main thread.

So the plain idiom works as it is, for one recipient or several:

'ENCRYPTION': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
    # 'age1abc...', or 'age1abc..., age1def...' — or nothing, on a laptop
    'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENTS', ''),
},

RECIPIENTS takes a string or a list. A string is split on commas and newlines, and — for age1… keys only — on whitespace; an ssh-ed25519 … recipient keeps the space inside it. On a machine with the store credentials and no recipient, E001 names RECIPIENTS.

docs.title: ENABLED: off, on, or refused
docs.text:
Three states, never confused:

  • off — OFFSITE_BACKUP is absent or empty, ENABLED is false, or none of the options that name a destination is set. Commands print "not configured on this machine, nothing to do" and exit 0; the system checks say nothing. A development machine holds no key — not giving it one is the enforcement.
  • partly configured — something says "back up" and something it needs is empty. Every missing piece is named by E001, and a pass refuses to start. It is never read as "off": a production machine that lost one variable must not stop backing up in silence.
  • on — every backend builds and every required option is set.

With ENABLED left at None (the default) the machine is on when any of these is non-empty:

backend options that switch it on S3Store BUCKET, ACCESS_KEY, SECRET_KEY, ENDPOINT_URL DirectoryStore ROOT

A recipient is not among them: it is a public key, and writing it into settings must not switch on every machine that has no store key. A machine with only the age recipient set — and no store credentials — is off, not partly configured. A hand-written predecessor may have used the recipient as its "on" switch; here the store is the switch.

A BACKEND path that does not import also counts as "on", so E002 can say what is wrong with it. ENABLED: True or False overrides the rule either way.

A recipient alone is off

A public key is not a secret, so RECIPIENTS: ['age1...'] may be written straight into settings.py. It switches nothing on: developer laptops and CI that load those settings without store credentials stay off, and manage.py check says nothing there. The other way round — store credentials and no recipient — is partly configured, and E001 names RECIPIENTS.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
Every key of offsite_backup.conf.DEFAULTS. RETENTION, CHECK, GUARD and DRILL merge with their defaults key by key, so 'GUARD': {'CACHE': 'redis'} keeps RUNNING_SECONDS; every other key replaces its default whole.

key type default what it is validated by ENABLED bool or None None on/off; None decides from the options above — PREFIX str '' every key lives under <PREFIX>/; rotation never leaves it. Surrounding / are stripped. Required E001 ENV str '' the environment, for the message's hashtag (#prod) — NAME str '' a service name; shown in a message only when PREFIX is empty — STORE block, or a list of blocks None where backups are kept — S3 or a directory; a list writes every pass to several stores, each with a NAME. Required E001, E002 ENCRYPTION block None how they are sealed — Encryption: the age binary or pyrage. Required E001, E002, E008 DATABASES block None Databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB or SQLite E001, E002, E009/W005 (deploy, SQLite) MEDIA list of blocks (or one block) [] Media E001, E002, E009, E012, W005 (deploy) CONFIG block None Configuration archive E002, E009, W005 (deploy) COMPRESS list of str (argv) ['zstd', '-19', '--long=27', '-T0', '-q'] the compression stage for databases and the configuration archive; empty turns compression off E003 (zstd on PATH when non-empty) DECOMPRESS list of str (argv) ['zstd', '-d', '-q', '--long=31'] the stage a restore runs on anything that starts with zstd's magic bytes — RETENTION dict {'KEEP_NIGHTS': 14} Retention E001, E007 CHECK dict {'STALE_HOURS': 26} Monitoring — NOTIFY list of blocks [] Notifications E002, W004 MESSAGES dotted path 'offsite_backup.messages.default' the formatter — Notifications — GUARD dict see below the once-per-night claim — Scheduling E001, W003 LAST_SUCCESS_FILE path '' a file rewritten with the ISO time of every successful pass — Monitoring — DEFAULT_REASON str 'manual' the reason backup_offsite uses when --reason is not given — Deploy integration — STRICT bool False every CONFIG path and every media source is required, and an unreadable file fails the pass — below E009 WORKDIR path '' where the temporary workspace is made — a pass's, a restore's, a drill's; '' is the system's temporary directory — DRILL dict see below the restore drill — Restore E011 (deploy)

At least one of DATABASES, MEDIA and CONFIG must be set, or E001 says "nothing to back up".

docs.title: RETENTION
docs.text: key type default KEEP_NIGHTS positive int 14 whole UTC nights kept per kind. Must be greater than the store's LOCK_DAYS (E007); not a positive integer is E001. A store's own KEEP_NIGHTS overrides it for that store

docs.title: CHECK
docs.text: key type default STALE_HOURS number 26 how old the newest whole backup may be before the morning check calls it missing

docs.title: GUARD
docs.text: key type default ENABLED bool True whether run_nightly() claims the night at all BACKEND 'cache' or 'database' 'cache' where the night is claimed: a shared Django cache, or a PostgreSQL advisory lock (Scheduling); anything else is E001 CACHE cache alias 'default' cache backend: must exist in CACHES (E001) and be shared between workers (W003 on LocMemCache and DummyCache) RUNNING_SECONDS int 3600 cache backend: how long a pass whose worker died holds the night DONE_SECONDS int 93600 (26 h) cache backend: how long "done" is remembered — past the end of its UTC date DATABASE database alias 'default' database backend: the database the lock is taken on; an alias that is not a PostgreSQL database in DATABASES is E001

docs.title: DRILL
docs.text: key type default DATABASE database alias '' the throwaway database every dump is restored into — an alias in DATABASES (or the source's CONNECTIONS). Required for a drill of a backup that holds databases. The same alias as a live one, or one that reaches the same host, port and database name, is refused — and is E011 under check --deploy, as is an alias that names no database IDENTITY_FILE path '' the age identity the drill decrypts with, when --identity is not given; '' falls back to AGE_IDENTITY MEDIA bool True decrypt and list every media volume too (--without-media turns it off for one run) COMPARE_LIVE bool True count the live databases too, and show both figures

docs.title: STRICT and REQUIRED
docs.text:
By default a pass backs up what is there: a missing CONFIG path is logged and left out, an unreadable file is logged and left out, and a media source with no files writes no volume. A deployment whose certificates or signing keys are part of what restores the machine may want a pass without them to fail instead. Two settings, one mechanism:

  • REQUIRED on a source, for that source only:
    • on CONFIG, True makes every path in PATHS required, and a list names the required ones ('REQUIRED': ['/app/deploy/certs']). A required path missing at pass time fails the pass;
    • on a media source, True makes a source with no files at all a failure.
  • STRICT: True at the top level, for the whole pass: every CONFIG path and every media source is required, and a file that cannot be read — a CONFIG file, or a file under a DirectorySource ROOT — fails the pass instead of being left out.

The pass fails with SourceMissingError, and the FAILED message names what was missing:

SourceMissingError: OFFSITE_BACKUP['CONFIG']: required path(s) missing: /app/deploy/certs

manage.py check --deploy reports a required CONFIG path missing where it runs as E009, and an optional one as W005; a plain manage.py check says nothing about paths (System checks).
